nodes.name: Cardinality of complete linear systems on graphs
nodes.statement: The purpose of this paper is to answer the question: What is the cardinality of the complete linear system~$|D|$ for each divisor~$D$? In other words, how many winning states are there for each dollar game on~$G$? This question was proposed by Haase, Musiker, and Yu at the end of their study \cite{Haase} of linear systems on tropical curves.
nodes.statement_short: Determine $\#|D|$, the number of effective divisors linearly equivalent to $D$, for every divisor $D$ on a graph.

nodes.name: Binary necklaces with n black and k white beads
nodes.statement: Let~$\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ denote the set of binary necklaces with~$n$ black beads and~$k$ white beads.

nodes.name: Graph G
nodes.statement: Let~$G=(V,\mathcal{E})$ be a connected, undirected multigraph with finite vertex set~$V$ and finite edge multiset~$\mathcal{E}$.

nodes.name: Fixed vertex q
nodes.statement: Many of our constructions will depend on fixing a vertex~$q\in V$, which we do now, once and for all.

nodes.name: Natural numbers
nodes.statement: We let~$\mathbb{N}:=\mathbb{Z}_{\geq0}$ denote the natural numbers.

nodes.name: Divisor on a graph
nodes.statement: A~{\em divisor} on~$G$ is an element of the free abelian group on the vertices of~$G$, \[ \mathrm{Div}(G):=\mathbb{Z} V=\textstyle\left\{ \sum_{v\in V}D(v)v:D(v)\in\mathbb{Z} \right\}. \]
nodes.genus: element of the free abelian group on the vertices of~$G$
also_stated_at: By definition, a {\em divisor}~$D$ is an element of ~$\mathbb{Z} V$, the free abelian group on the vertices of~$G$.

nodes.name: Degree of a divisor
nodes.statement: The~{degree} of a divisor~$D$ is the sum of its coefficients:~$\deg(D):=\sum_{v\in V}D(v)$.
also_stated_at: The net amount of money on the graph is the {\em degree},~$\deg(D):=\sum_{v\in V}D(v)$, of~$D$.

nodes.name: Vertex degree
nodes.statement: We use the notation~$\deg_G(v)$ to refer to the ordinary degree of a vertex---the number of edges incident on~$v$.

nodes.name: Divisors of degree k
nodes.statement: The set of divisors of degree~$k$ is denoted by~$\mathrm{Div}^k(G)$.

nodes.name: Discrete Laplacian operator
nodes.statement: The {\em (discrete) Laplacian operator} of~$G$ is the function~$L\colon\mathbb{Z}^V\to\mathbb{Z}^V$ given by \[ L(f)(v)=\sum_{vw\in \mathcal{E}}\left( f(v)-f(w) \right) \] for each $f\in\mathbb{Z}^V$ and~$v\in V$.

nodes.name: Divisor of a function
nodes.statement: The {\em divisor of a function}~$f\colon V\to\mathbb{Z}$, arising by analogy from the theory of divisors on Riemann surfaces, is then \[ \mathrm{div}(f):=\sum_{v\in V}\left( L(f)(v) \right)v\in\mathrm{Div}(G). \]

nodes.name: Principal divisors
nodes.statement: Divisors of functions are called {\em principal divisors}, and they form an additive subgroup of~$\mathrm{Div}(G)$ denoted~$\mathrm{Prin}(G)$.

nodes.name: Linear equivalence of divisors
nodes.statement: Two divisors~$D$ and~$D'$ are {\em linearly equivalent} if~$D-D'\in\mathrm{Prin}(G)$, in which case, we write~$D\sim D'$.
also_stated_at: Two divisors are {\em linearly equivalent} if one may be transformed into the other by a sequence of lending and borrowing moves.

nodes.name: Picard group
nodes.statement: The {\em Picard group} of~$G$ is then the group of divisors modulo linear equivalence: \[ \mathrm{Pic}(G):=\mathrm{Div}(G)/\mathrm{Prin}(G). \]
also_stated_at: The {\em Picard group},~$\mathrm{Pic}(G)$, is the group of divisors modulo linear equivalence.

nodes.name: Degree-k part of the Picard group
nodes.statement: Its degree~$k$ part is denoted~$\mathrm{Pic}^k(G)$.

nodes.name: Jacobian group
nodes.statement: The degree-zero part of the Picard group is a subgroup called the {\em Jacobian group} of~$G$: \[ \mathrm{Jac}(G):=\mathrm{Pic}^0(G)=\mathrm{Div}^0(G)/\mathrm{Prin}(G)\subseteq\mathrm{Pic}(G). \]
also_stated_at: Its degree~$0$ part is a finite group called the {\em Jacobian group},~$\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, and there is an isomorphism~$\mathrm{Pic}(G)\simeq\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, depending on the choice of a vertex (cf.~\eqref{eqn: Pic(G)}).

nodes.name: Divisor class
nodes.statement: We write~$[D]$ for the class of a divisor~$D$ modulo~$\mathrm{Prin}(G)$.

nodes.name: Isomorphism Pic(G) to Z plus Jac(G)
nodes.statement: \mathrm{Pic}(G)&\to\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathrm{Jac}(G)\\ [D]&\mapsto\left(\deg(D), [D-\deg(D)q] \right).\nonumber
nodes.label: eqn: Pic(G)

nodes.name: Vertex ordering and identification with Z^n
nodes.statement: Fixing an ordering~$v_1,\dots,v_n$ of~$V$ determines a basis for~$\mathrm{Div}(G)$ and a corresponding dual basis for~$\mathbb{Z}^V$, allowing us to identify both spaces with~$\mathbb{Z}^n$.

nodes.name: Laplacian matrix
nodes.statement: With respect to the chosen bases,~$\mathrm{div}$ and~$L$ are represented by the~$n\times n$ {\em Laplacian matrix}, which we also denote by~$L$.

nodes.name: Laplacian matrix formula
nodes.statement: This matrix is given by \[ L=\mathrm{Deg}(G)-A \] where $\mathrm{Deg}(G)=\mathrm{diag}(\deg_G(v_1),\dots,\deg_G(v_n))$ and~$A$ is the adjacency matrix for~$G$ with~$i,j$-th entry equal to the number of edges connecting~$v_i$ to~$v_j$.

nodes.name: Reduced Laplacian
nodes.statement: The {\em reduced Laplacian} matrix for~$G$ with respect to~$q$ is the~$(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrix~$\tilde{L}$ formed by removing the row and column corresponding to~$q$ from~$L$.

nodes.name: Restriction D|_{q=0} and the isomorphism for Jac(G)
nodes.statement: There is an isomorphism \begin{align} \mathrm{Jac}(G)&\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}/\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\tilde{L})\\ [D]&\to D|_{q=0}\nonumber \end{align} where~$D|_{q=0}:=\sum_{v\in V\setminus\left\{ q \right\}}D(v)v$.

nodes.name: Isomorphism Jac(G) to Z^{n-1}/im(reduced Laplacian)
nodes.statement: \mathrm{Jac}(G)&\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}/\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\tilde{L})\\ [D]&\to D|_{q=0}\nonumber
nodes.label: eqn: Jac(G)

nodes.name: Criterion for linear equivalence
nodes.statement: Isomorphisms~\ref{eqn: Pic(G)} and~\ref{eqn: Jac(G)} combine to say that for~$D,D'\in\mathrm{Div}(G)$, \[ D\sim D' \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \left( \deg(D)=\deg(D') \quad\text{and}\quad D|_{q=0}=D'|_{q=0}\bmod\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\tilde{L})\right). \]
conclusions: D\sim D' \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \left( \deg(D)=\deg(D') \quad\text{and}\quad D|_{q=0}=D'|_{q=0}\bmod\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\tilde{L})\right)

nodes.name: Kernel of the Laplacian and rank of the reduced Laplacian
nodes.statement: The kernel of the Laplacian matrix is the set of constant vectors, and the reduced Laplacian has full rank~$n-1$.
conclusions: The kernel of the Laplacian matrix is the set of constant vectors
the reduced Laplacian has full rank~$n-1$

nodes.name: Matrix-tree theorem
nodes.statement: By the matrix-tree theorem, the number of spanning trees of~$G$ is~$\det(\tilde{L})$, and thus by~$\eqref{eqn: Jac(G)}$, it is also the order of~$\mathrm{Jac}(G)$.
conclusions: the number of spanning trees of~$G$ is~$\det(\tilde{L})$
it is also the order of~$\mathrm{Jac}(G)$

nodes.name: Order of a vertex
nodes.statement: We adopt the following notation: for each~$v\in V$, let \[ \mathrm{ord}_q(v):= \text{order of~$[v-q]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$}. \]

nodes.name: Set firing
nodes.statement: A {\em set firing} by a subset $W\subseteq V$ on a divisor~$D$ produces a new divisor~$D'=D-\mathrm{div}(\chi_W)$ where~$\chi_W$ is the characteristic function of~$W$.

nodes.name: Legal set firing
nodes.statement: Firing a set~$W$ is {\em legal} if~$D'(w)\geq0$ for all~$w\in W$.

nodes.name: q-reduced divisor
nodes.statement: The divisor~$D$ is~{\em $q$-reduced} if \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] $D(v)\geq 0$ for all~$v\in V\setminus\left\{ q \right\}$, and \item[(ii)] $D$ has no legal set firing by a nonempty set $W\subseteq V\setminus\left\{ q \right\}$. \end{enumerate}
differentia: $D$ has no legal set firing by a nonempty set $W\subseteq V\setminus\left\{ q \right\}$

nodes.name: Existence and uniqueness of q-reduced divisors
nodes.statement: It turns out that each divisor is linearly equivalent to a unique~$q$-reduced divisor.
conclusions: each divisor is linearly equivalent to a unique~$q$-reduced divisor

nodes.name: Degree bound for q-reduced divisors
nodes.statement: If~$D$ is $q$-reduced, then letting~$\deg(D|_{q=0}):=\sum_{v\in V\setminus\left\{ q \right\}}D(v)$ we have \[ 0\leq\deg(D|_{q=0})\leq |\mathcal{E}|-|V|+1. \]
conclusions: 0\leq\deg(D|_{q=0})\leq |\mathcal{E}|-|V|+1.

nodes.name: Effective divisor
nodes.statement: A divisor~$E$ is {\em effective} if~$E(v)\geq0$ for all~$v\in V$, in which case we write~$E\geq0$.
also_stated_at: Such a debt-free divisor is said to be {\em effective}.

nodes.name: Complete linear system
nodes.statement: The {\em complete linear system} of a divisor~$D$ is its set of linearly equivalent effective divisors: \[ |D| := \left\{ E\in\mathrm{Div}(G): E\geq 0\text{ and } E\sim D \right\}. \]
also_stated_at: The {\em complete linear system} of a divisor~$D$, denoted~$|D|$, is the set of all effective divisors linearly equivalent to~$D$.

nodes.name: Complete linear systems are finite
nodes.statement: Also, since linearly equivalent divisors have the same degree,~$|D|$ is finite.
conclusions: $|D|$ is finite

nodes.name: The set E_[D]
nodes.statement: For each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, define \[ \mathbb{E}_{[D]}:=\cup_{k\geq0}|D+kq|=\left\{ E\in\mathrm{Div}(G):E\geq0\text{ and } E-\deg(E)q\sim D \right\}. \]
also_stated_at: To answer it, we first use the isomorphism~$\mathrm{Pic}(G)\simeq\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ to partition the collection of all effective divisors on~$G$ into sets~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$, one for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$.

nodes.name: The sets E_[D] partition the effective divisors
nodes.statement: The~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ partition the set of effective divisors as~$D$ runs over a set of representatives for~$\mathrm{Jac}(G)$.
conclusions: The~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ partition the set of effective divisors

nodes.name: E_[0] is a commutative monoid acting on E_[D]
nodes.statement: The collection~$\mathbb{E}_{[0]}$ is a commutative monoid, and it acts on each~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ via addition: $\mathbb{E}_{[0]}+\mathbb{E}_{[D]}=\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$.
conclusions: The collection~$\mathbb{E}_{[0]}$ is a commutative monoid
it acts on each~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ via addition

nodes.name: lambda-sequence and its generating function
nodes.statement: The~$\lambda$-sequence for~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ is the sequence with~$k$-th term \[ \lambda_{[D]}(k):=\#|D+kq|. \] (It does not depend on the choice of representative of the class~$[D]$.) The generating function for the~$\lambda$-sequence is \[ \Lambda_{[D]}(z):=\sum_{k\geq0}\lambda_{[D]}(k)z^k. \]
also_stated_at: Let~$\lambda_{[D]}(k)$ be the number of divisors in~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ with degree~$k$, and let~$\Lambda_{[D]}(z):=\sum_{k\geq0}\lambda_{[D]}(k)z^k$ be its generating function.
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda_{[D]}(k)$ counts the complete linear system $|D+kq|$; $\Lambda_{[D]}$ is its ordinary generating function.

nodes.name: Primary and secondary divisors theorem
nodes.statement: \ \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*] \item {\rm (Existence)} There exists a finite subset $\mathcal{P}\subset\mathbb{E}_{[0]}$ and for each $[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, a finite subset $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}\subset\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ such that each $E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ can be written uniquely as \[ E = F + \sum_{P\in\mathcal{P}}a_P P \] with $F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ and~$a_P\in\mathbb{N}$ for all~$P\in\mathcal{P}$. The set $\mathcal{P}$ is called a set of {\em primary divisors} for~$G$, and $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ is called the set of {\em $[D]$-secondary} divisors with respect to~$\mathcal{P}$. \item {\rm (Uniqueness)} Sets~$\mathcal{P}$ and~$\{\mathcal{S}_{[D]}\}_{[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)}$ satisfy part~\ref{ps-1} if and only if \[ \mathcal{P}=\left\{\ell_v v: v\in V\right\} \quad\text{and}\quad \mathcal{S}_{[D]}=\{E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}:E(v)<\ell_v \mbox{ for all $v\in V$}\}, \] where~$\ell_v$ is a positive multiple of~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ for all~$v\in V$. In particular, taking~$\ell_v=\mathrm{ord}_q(v)$ for all~$v\in V$ produces the set of primary divisors of smallest degree and corresponding sets of secondary divisors with minimal cardinality. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Each $E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ decomposes uniquely as a secondary divisor plus an $\mathbb{N}$-combination of primary divisors $\ell_v v$, with $\ell_v$ a multiple of $\mathrm{ord}_q(v)$, and these are the only such systems.
conclusions: There exists a finite subset $\mathcal{P}\subset\mathbb{E}_{[0]}$ and for each $[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, a finite subset $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}\subset\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ such that each $E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ can be written uniquely as \[ E = F + \sum_{P\in\mathcal{P}}a_P P \] with $F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ and~$a_P\in\mathbb{N}$ for all~$P\in\mathcal{P}$.

Sets~$\mathcal{P}$ and~$\{\mathcal{S}_{[D]}\}_{[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)}$ satisfy part~\ref{ps-1} if and only if \[ \mathcal{P}=\left\{\ell_v v: v\in V\right\} \quad\text{and}\quad \mathcal{S}_{[D]}=\{E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}:E(v)<\ell_v \mbox{ for all $v\in V$}\}, \] where~$\ell_v$ is a positive multiple of~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ for all~$v\in V$.

There exists a finite subset $\mathcal{P}\subset\mathbb{E}_{[0]}$ and for each $[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, a finite subset $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}\subset\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ such that each $E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ can be written uniquely as \[ E = F + \sum_{P\in\mathcal{P}}a_P P \] with $F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ and~$a_P\in\mathbb{N}$ for all~$P\in\mathcal{P}$.

Sets~$\mathcal{P}$ and~$\{\mathcal{S}_{[D]}\}_{[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)}$ satisfy part~\ref{ps-1} if and only if \[ \mathcal{P}=\left\{\ell_v v: v\in V\right\} \quad\text{and}\quad \mathcal{S}_{[D]}=\{E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}:E(v)<\ell_v \mbox{ for all $v\in V$}\}, \] where~$\ell_v$ is a positive multiple of~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ for all~$v\in V$.

equivalent_conditions: \mathcal{P}=\left\{\ell_v v: v\in V\right\} \quad\text{and}\quad \mathcal{S}_{[D]}=\{E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}:E(v)<\ell_v \mbox{ for all $v\in V$}\}, \] where~$\ell_v$ is a positive multiple of~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ for all~$v\in V$.
nodes.label: thm: primary-secondary

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: To prove part~\ref{ps-1}, for each~$v\in V$, let~$\ell_v$ be a positive multiple of~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$, and define~$\mathcal{P}$ and each~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ as in part~\ref{ps-2} of the theorem. Given~$E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$, for each~$v\in V$, let~$k_v$ be the largest integer such that~$E(v)-k_v\ell_v\geq0$, and define~$F:=E-\sum_{v\in V}k_v\ell_vv\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$. Then $E=F+\sum_{v\in V}k_v\ell_vv$ is a decomposition as required in part~\ref{ps-1}. For uniqueness of this decomposition, suppose $E = F' + \sum_{v\in V}k_v'v$ for some~$F'\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ and~$k'_v\in\mathbb{N}$. Then for each~$v\in V$, we have~$0\leq F(v)=E(v)- k_v\ell_v<\ell_v$ and~$0\leq F'(v)=E(v)-k'_v\ell_v<\ell_v$. Subtracting these inequalities yields $-\ell_v<(k'_v-k_v)\ell_v<\ell_v$. It follows that~$k_v=k'_v$ for all~$v$ and~$F=F'$. We have shown that if~$\mathcal{P}$ and~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ have the form displayed in~$\ref{ps-2}$, then they serve as sets of primary and secondary divisors, i.e., they satisfy the conditions in part~\ref{ps-1}. To show that necessity of this form and thus finish the proof of part~\ref{ps-2}, let~$\mathcal{P}$ and~$\{\mathcal{S}_{[D]}\}_{[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)}$ be any sets of primary and~$[D]$-secondary divisors. Since~$\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ is finite, for each~$v\in V$, there is a smallest natural number~$m_v$ such that~$m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v\notin\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$. Consider the primary-secondary decomposition~$m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v=F+\sum_{P\in\mathcal{P}}a_PP$. Since the divisors on the right-hand side are effective and all~$a_P$ are nonnegative, considering coefficients on both sides, it follows that decomposition takes the form~$m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v=av+bv$ for some~$a,b\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $av\in\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ and $bv\in\mathcal{P}$. By definition of~$m_v$, we must have~$b>0$. Since~$\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ and~$\mathcal{P}$ are subsets of~$\mathbb{E}_{[0]}$, we have~$av\sim aq$ and~$bv\sim bq$. Therefore,~$a=a'\mathrm{ord}(v)$ and~$b=b'\mathrm{ord}(v)$ for some~$a',b'\in\mathbb{N}$. If~$a'\neq0$, then~$b'<m_v$, which implies~$b'\mathrm{ord}(v)v\in\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ by definition of~$m_v$. However, that is impossible since the uniqueness of decompositions described in part~\ref{ps-1} implies~$\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ and~$\mathcal{P}$ are disjoint. Defining~$\ell_v:=m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)$, it follows that~$\ell_v v\in\mathcal{P}$ for all~$v$. However, again by uniqueness of decompositions, the elements of~$\mathcal{P}$ must be linearly independent over~$\mathbb{Z}$, which implies there are no other primary divisors. So~$\mathcal{P}=\left\{ \ell_v:v\in V \right\}$, as claimed, and it is then straightforward to show that~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ must have the form stated in~\ref{ps-2} for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Existence and uniqueness by division with remainder of each coefficient by $\ell_v$; necessity by examining the decomposition of minimal multiples $m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v\notin\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$.

nodes.name: Rational generating function via primary and secondary divisors
nodes.statement: Fix primary and secondary divisors as in Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}. For each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, \[ \Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\frac{S(z)}{\prod_{v\in V}\left(1-z^{\ell_v}\right)} \] where \[ S(z)=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}}z^{\deg(F)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: $\Lambda_{[D]}(z)$ equals the secondary-divisor degree polynomial divided by $\prod_v(1-z^{\ell_v})$.
assumptions: Fix primary and secondary divisors as in Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}.
conclusions: \Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\frac{S(z)}{\prod_{v\in V}\left(1-z^{\ell_v}\right)}
nodes.label: cor: ps-genfun

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.2
nodes.statement: Introduce indeterminates~$\left\{ x_v \right\}_{v\in V}$, and identify each effective divisor~$E$ with a monomial~$x^E:=\prod_{v\in V}x_v^{E(v)}$. Define \[ \sigma_D(x)=\sum_{E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}}x^{E}. \] By Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}, we may uniquely write \[ x^E=x^F\cdot\prod_{P\in\mathcal{P}}x^{a_PP} =x^F\cdot\prod_{v\in V}x_v^{a_v\ell_v} \] for some~$F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ and~$a_v\geq0$. Then \begin{align*} \sigma_D(x)&=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}}x^F\sum_{a\in \mathbb{N}^V}\prod_{v\in V}x_v^{a_v\ell_v} =\left(\sum_{F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}}x^F\right)\prod_{v\in V}\left(1+x_v^{\ell_v}+x_v^{2\ell_v} +\dots\right)\\[8pt] &=\left(\sum_{F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}}x^F\right)\prod_{v\in V}\frac{1}{1-x_v^{\ell_v}}. \end{align*} Now note that $\Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\sigma_D(z,z,\dots,z)$ to conclude the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Write the multivariate generating series of $\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ via the unique decomposition, sum geometric series, then specialize all variables to $z$.

nodes.name: Sum of secondary numerators over Jac(G)
nodes.statement: Denote the numerator~$S$ in Corollary~\ref{cor: ps-genfun} by~$S_{[D]}(z)$ to indicate its dependence on $[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$. Since the~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ partition the set of effective divisors, it follows that~$\sum_{[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)}\Lambda_{[D]}(z)=1/(1-z)^n$, and hence, \[ \sum_{[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)}S_{[D]}(z)=\frac{\prod_{v\in V}(1-z^{\ell_v})}{(1-z)^n}=\prod_{v\in V}(1+z+z^2+\dots+z^{\ell_v-1}). \]
nodes.statement_short: Summing $\Lambda_{[D]}$ over $\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ gives $1/(1-z)^n$, so the numerators sum to $\prod_v(1+z+\dots+z^{\ell_v-1})$.
nodes.label: remark: ps-comp

nodes.name: Natural projection pi
nodes.statement: Fix primary and secondary divisors as in Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}~\ref{ps-2}, and consider the natural projection \[ \pi\colon \mathrm{Div}(G)=\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{Z}^n/\prod_{v\in V}\ell_v\mathbb{Z}. \]

nodes.name: Standard representative
nodes.statement: A {\em standard representative} of an element~$\overline{D}\in\mathbb{Z}^n/\prod_{v\in V}\ell_v\mathbb{Z}$ is a divisor~$E\in\mathrm{Div}(G)$ such that~$\pi(E)=\overline{D}$ and~$0\leq E(v)<\ell_v$ for all~$v$.

nodes.name: Vertex q is last in the ordering
nodes.statement: Assume vertex~$q$ appears last in the ordering so that \[ \mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}\times\mathbb{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{Z}=\mathbb{Z}^n=\mathrm{Div}(G). \]

nodes.name: The set H_[D]
nodes.statement: For each~$D\in\mathrm{Div}(G)$, define \[ H_{[D]}:=\pi(D+(\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}\times\mathbb{Z}))\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n/\prod_{v\in V}\ell_v\mathbb{Z}. \]

nodes.name: Computation of primary and secondary divisors
nodes.statement: Let~$\mathcal{P}=\left\{ \ell_v v:v\in V \right\}$ and~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ be as in Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}~\ref{ps-2}. \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*] \item Let~$\tilde{L}^{-1}$ be the inverse of the reduced Laplacian over~$\mathbb{Q}$. Then, for each~$v\neq q$, the integer~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ is the least common multiple of the denominators of the (reduced) fractions in the~$v$-th column of~$\tilde{L}^{-1}$. \item For each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, there is a bijection of sets \begin{align*} \mathcal{S}_{[D]}&\to H_{[D]}\\ E&\mapsto\pi(E|_{q=0},\deg(E)), \end{align*} and thus~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ is exactly a set of standard representatives for~$H_{[D]}$. \item For each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, \[ |\mathcal{S}_{[D]}||\mathrm{Jac}(G)|=\prod_{v\in V}\ell_v. \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{ord}_q(v)$ is the lcm of denominators in the $v$-th column of $\tilde{L}^{-1}$; $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ are standard representatives of $H_{[D]}$; $|\mathcal{S}_{[D]}||\mathrm{Jac}(G)|=\prod\ell_v$.
assumptions: Let~$\mathcal{P}=\left\{ \ell_v v:v\in V \right\}$ and~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ be as in Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}~\ref{ps-2}.
conclusions: Then, for each~$v\neq q$, the integer~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ is the least common multiple of the denominators of the (reduced) fractions in the~$v$-th column of~$\tilde{L}^{-1}$.
and thus~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ is exactly a set of standard representatives for~$H_{[D]}$.
|\mathcal{S}_{[D]}||\mathrm{Jac}(G)|=\prod_{v\in V}\ell_v.
nodes.label: prop: ps-computation

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.4
nodes.statement: First note that~$\tilde{L}$ has rank~$n-1$, and thus has an inverse~$\tilde{L}^{-1}$ over~$\mathbb{Q}$. By~\eqref{eqn: Jac(G)} of Section~\ref{sect: prelims}, the order of~$[v-q]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ is the least positive integer~$k$ such that~$kv\in\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}$. Therefore,~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ is the least positive integer~$k$ such that~$\tilde{L}^{-1}(kv)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$. Part~\ref{ps-comp1} follows. Part~\ref{ps-comp2} is immediate: a divisor~$E$ is a standard representative for an element in~$H_{[D]}$ if and only if $E|_{q=0}=D|_{q=0} \bmod\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}$ and $0\leq E(v)<\ell_v$ for all~$v\in V$, which is exactly the requirement for being an element of~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$. Now consider part~\ref{ps-comp3}. Since~$\ell_v[v-q]=[0]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ for all~$v$, there is a surjection \[ \textstyle {\mathbb{Z}}^n/\prod_{v\in V}\ell_v\mathbb{Z}\to\mathrm{Jac}(G)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}/\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L} \] which sends the class of the~$v$-th standard basis vector to~$[v-q]$. Its kernel is~$H_{[0]}$. So by part~\ref{ps-comp2}, we have $|\mathcal{S}_{[0]}||\mathrm{Jac}(G)|=\prod_{v\in V}\ell_v$. However, for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, there is a well-defined bijection \begin{align*} H_{[0]}&\to H_{[D]}\\ \pi(E)&\mapsto\pi(D+E). \end{align*} So~$|\mathcal{S}_{[D]}|=|\mathcal{S}_{[0]}|$, and part~\ref{ps-comp3} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Part (1) from the description of $\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ via $\tilde{L}$; (2) by unwinding definitions; (3) via the surjection onto $\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ with kernel $H_{[0]}$ and translation bijections.

nodes.name: Computation of primary and secondary divisors (method)
nodes.statement: (Computation of primary and secondary divisors) To summarize the above: in order to compute a set of primary divisors, use Proposition~\ref{prop: ps-computation} to compute each~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ for~$v\neq q$ from the columns of~$\tilde{L}^{-1}$. Then take~$\mathcal{P}=\{ \ell_v v \}_{v\in V}$ where the~$\ell_v$ are arbitrary positive multiples of the corresponding~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$. In order to minimize the number of secondary divisors, one would take~$\ell_v=\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ for each~$v$. In particular, this would mean~$\ell_q=\mathrm{ord}_{q}(q)=1$. Next, use part~\ref{ps-comp2} of Proposition~\ref{prop: ps-computation} to compute~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$. To ease the computation of~$\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}$, perform invertible integer column operations on~$\tilde{L}$ to compute its Hermite normal form~$A$. (We will always take ``Hermite normal form'' to mean ``column Hermite normal form''.) Then find the set~$S$ of standard representatives for the coset $D|_{q=0}+\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}A$ modulo $\prod_{v\in V\setminus\left\{ q \right\}}\ell_v\mathbb{Z}$. Finally~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}=\left\{ c+kq:c\in S \text{ and } 0\leq k <\ell_q\right\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute orders from columns of $\tilde{L}^{-1}$ to get primary divisors, then secondary divisors as standard representatives of cosets of the Hermite normal form image.
nodes.label: remark: method

nodes.name: Trees (primary-secondary)
nodes.statement: If~$G$ is a tree, then~$\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ is trivial, and the mapping~$[D]\mapsto\deg(D)$ is an isomorphism of~$\mathrm{Pic}(G)$ with~$\mathbb{Z}$. It follows that for any~$q\in V$, \[ \mathbb{E}_{[0]} = \cup_{k\geq 0}|kq| = \left\{ E\in\mathrm{Div}(G):E\geq0 \text{ and } \deg(E)\geq0 \right\}. \] So, letting~$n=|V|$, the cardinality of~$|kq|$ is the number of elements of~$\mathbb{N}^n$ with coordinate sum equal to~$k$. Thus, \[ \Lambda_{[0]}(z)=\sum_{k\geq 0}\binom{n-1+k}{k}z^k=\frac{1}{(1-z)^n}, \] in agreement with Corollary~\ref{cor: ps-genfun} where we take~$\ell_v=1$ for all~$v\in V$. In that case~$\mathcal{P}=V$ and~$\mathcal{S}_{[0]}=\left\{ 0 \right\}$.
nodes.statement_short: For a tree, $\Lambda_{[0]}(z)=1/(1-z)^n$ with $\mathcal{P}=V$ and $\mathcal{S}_{[0]}=\{0\}$.

nodes.name: Diamond graph (primary-secondary)
nodes.statement_short: Diamond graph: orders $(8,8,2,1)$, 16 secondary divisors per class, explicit $\Lambda_{[0]}$ and $\Lambda_{[v_1-q]}$.

nodes.name: Cycle graphs (primary-secondary)
nodes.statement_short: Cycle graph $C_n$: primary divisors $nv_i$ and $q$, explicit secondary divisors, and the $C_4$, $j=2$ generating function.

nodes.name: Jacobian of the cycle graph
nodes.statement: It is well-known that~$\mathrm{Jac}(C_n)\simeq\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, with generator~$D_1:=[v_1-q]$ and such that $D_j:=[v_{j}-q]=j[v_1-q]$ for all~$j$, where the indices are determined modulo~$n$.
conclusions: $\mathrm{Jac}(C_n)\simeq\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, with generator~$D_1:=[v_1-q]$
also_stated_at: Then~$\mathrm{Jac}(C_n)$ is the cyclic group of order~$n$ generated by~$[D_1]$ with~$j[D_1]=[D_j]$ for all~$j$.

nodes.name: Complete graphs and parking functions (primary-secondary)
nodes.statement_short: Complete graph $K_n$: $n$ secondary divisors, first differences of $\lambda$ are concatenated binomials; maximal parking-function classes give repeated binomials.

nodes.name: First differences of the lambda-sequence on K_n
nodes.statement: A bit of calculation then shows that writing~$k=an+b$ in terms of quotient and remainder by~$n$ gives \[ \Delta\lambda_{[0]}(k)=\binom{a+b}{n-2}. \]
assumptions: writing~$k=an+b$ in terms of quotient and remainder by~$n$
conclusions: \Delta\lambda_{[0]}(k)=\binom{a+b}{n-2}.

nodes.name: Parking function
nodes.statement: A vector~$p=(p_1,\dots,p_{n-1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ with~$1\leq p_i\leq n$ for each~$i$ is a {\em parking function} of length~$n-1$ if for each~$j=1,\dots,n-1$, \[ |\left\{ i:p_i\leq j \right\}|\geq j. \]

nodes.name: q-reduced divisors on K_n are parking functions
nodes.statement: However, on~$K_n$ it turns out that a divisor $D$ is~$q$-reduced if and only if~$D|_{q=0}=p-\vec{1}=(p_1-1,\dots,p_{n-1}-1)$ for some parking function $p$.
conclusions: a divisor $D$ is~$q$-reduced if and only if~$D|_{q=0}=p-\vec{1}=(p_1-1,\dots,p_{n-1}-1)$ for some parking function $p$

nodes.name: First differences for maximal parking function classes on K_n
nodes.statement: An analysis like that given above for~$\lambda_{[0]}$ shows that the sequence of first differences of the~$\lambda$-sequence for~$[D]$ starts out with~$\binom{n-1}{2}$ zeroes and then is followed by the sequence~$\binom{k+n-2}{n-2}_{k\geq0}$ but with each term repeated~$n$ times.
conclusions: the sequence of first differences of the~$\lambda$-sequence for~$[D]$ starts out with~$\binom{n-1}{2}$ zeroes and then is followed by the sequence~$\binom{k+n-2}{n-2}_{k\geq0}$ but with each term repeated~$n$ times

nodes.name: Affine n-cone
nodes.statement: An {\em affine $n$-cone in~$\mathbb{R}^n$}, or simply, an {\em $n$-cone}, is a set of the form \[ \mathcal{K} = \left\{\, p+\lambda_1\omega_1+\dots+\lambda_m\omega_m:\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m\geq0 \right\}, \] where~$\omega_1,\dots,\omega_m,p\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and the span of the~$\omega_i$ has dimension~$n$.

nodes.name: Generators of a cone
nodes.statement: The~$\omega_i$ are called {\em generators} of the cone.

nodes.name: Extreme ray
nodes.statement: Any generator that is not a nonnegative combination of the remaining generators is called an {\em extreme ray}.

nodes.name: Pointed cone and apex
nodes.statement: The cone is {\em pointed} if it contains no line, and in that case~$p$ is called its {\em apex}.

nodes.name: Rational cone
nodes.statement: We say~$\mathcal{K}$ is {\em rational} if~$p,\omega_1,\dots,\omega_m\in\mathbb{Q}^n$, and then, by rescaling, we may assume the~$\omega_i$ have integer coordinates.

nodes.name: Simplicial cone
nodes.statement: An~$n$-cone is {\em simplicial} if it may be written using~$n$ generators.

nodes.name: Fundamental parallelepiped
nodes.statement: If~$\mathcal{K}$ is a simplicial~$n$-cone in~$\mathbb{R}^n$ with an integral generating set~$\Omega=\{\omega_1,\dots,\omega_n\}$ and apex~$p$, define the {\em fundamental parallelepiped} for~$\mathcal{K}$ with respect to~$\Omega$ to be \[ \textstyle \Pi:=\left\{\, p+\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\omega_i:0\leq\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_n<1 \right\}. \]

nodes.name: Unique decomposition of lattice points in a simplicial cone
nodes.statement: Every point~$\alpha\in\mathcal{K}\cap\mathbb{Z}^n$ has a unique expression as \[ \alpha = \pi+m_1\omega_1+\dots+m_d\omega_d \] with~$\pi\in\Pi$ and~$m_1,\dots,m_d\in\mathbb{N}$.
conclusions: has a unique expression as \[ \alpha = \pi+m_1\omega_1+\dots+m_d\omega_d \] with~$\pi\in\Pi$ and~$m_1,\dots,m_d\in\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.label: property: characterization

nodes.name: Integer-point transform
nodes.statement: Define the {\em integer-point transform} of a set~$S\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ by \[ \sigma_S(\vec{z}\,)=\sigma_S(z_1,\dots,z_n):=\sum_{\alpha\in S\cap\mathbb{Z}^n}\vec{z}^{\ \alpha}, \] where~$\vec{z}^{\ \alpha}:=\prod_{i=1}^nz_i^{\alpha_i}$.

nodes.name: Generating function of a simplicial cone
nodes.statement: {\rm (\cite[Theorem 3.5]{Beck})} Let \[ \mathcal{K} = \left\{\, p+\lambda_1\omega_1+\dots+\lambda_m\omega_n:\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\geq0 \right\} \] be a simplicial~$n$-cone in~$\mathbb{R}^n$ with~$\omega_1,\dots,\omega_n\in\mathbb{Z}^n$ and~$p\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Then \[ \sigma_{\mathcal{K}}(\vec{z}\,)=\frac{\sigma_{\Pi}(\vec{z}\,)}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-\vec{z}^{\ \omega_i})}, \] where~$\Pi$ is the fundamental parallelepiped of~$\mathcal{K}$ with respect to the~$\omega_i$.
nodes.statement_short: The integer-point transform of a simplicial cone is that of its fundamental parallelepiped divided by $\prod(1-z^{\omega_i})$.
conclusions: \sigma_{\mathcal{K}}(\vec{z}\,)=\frac{\sigma_{\Pi}(\vec{z}\,)}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-\vec{z}^{\ \omega_i})},
nodes.label: thm: polyhedral generating function

nodes.name: Firing script
nodes.statement: In this context~$f$ is referred to as a {\em firing script}, and we express the complete linear system for~$D$ as \[ |D|=\left\{ E\in\mathrm{Div}(G): E = D+Lf\geq0 \text{ for some firing script~$f$}\right\}. \]

nodes.name: Notation Lf for the embedded firing script
nodes.statement: Similarly, given~$f\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$, we write~$Lf$ in place of~$L\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}f\\0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.

nodes.name: Polyhedron Q_D
nodes.statement: The set of firing scripts appearing above for the complete linear system for~$D$ form the polyhedron \[ Q_D :=\left\{f\in\mathbb{R}^n: Lf\geq -D\right\}\subset\mathbb{R}^n. \]

nodes.name: Polytope P_D
nodes.statement: The kernel is generated by the all-ones vector~$\vec{1}$; so modulo~$\ker(L)$, each firing script~$f=(f_1,\dots,f_n)$ has the unique representative $f-f_n\cdot\vec{1}$ with last coordinate~$0$, leading us to define \[ P_D:=Q_D\cap\left\{f\in\mathbb{R}^n: f_n=0 \right\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n-1} \] so that~$Q_D=P_D+\mathbb{R}\vec{1}\subset\mathbb{R}^n$.

nodes.name: Lattice points of P_D are in bijection with |D|
nodes.statement: It is straightforward to see that the integer points~$P_D\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ are in bijection with~$|D|$: \begin{equation} f\in P_D\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad D+Lf\in|D|. \end{equation}
conclusions: the integer points~$P_D\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ are in bijection with~$|D|$

nodes.name: Bijection between lattice points of P_D and |D|
nodes.statement: f\in P_D\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad D+Lf\in|D|.
nodes.label: eqn: polytope bijection

nodes.name: P_D is a polytope
nodes.statement: Since~$|D|$ is finite, it follows that the polyhedron~$P_D$ is bounded, and hence is a~{\em polytope}.
conclusions: the polyhedron~$P_D$ is bounded
is a~{\em polytope}

nodes.name: Linearly equivalent divisors give translated polyhedra
nodes.statement: If~$D\sim D'$ with~$D'=D+Lf$, then the polyhedra associated with these divisors differ by a translation: $Q_{D}=f+Q_{D'}$, and as discussed above, we may assume~$f_n=0$ to write $P_{D}=f+P_{D'}$.
conclusions: the polyhedra associated with these divisors differ by a translation

nodes.name: q-cone of a divisor
nodes.statement: The {\em $q$-cone} for a divisor~$D\in\mathrm{Div}^0(G)$ is the set \[ \mathcal{K}_D := \left\{ (f,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R} : Lf+tq\geq -D \text{ and } f_n=0\right\} \subset\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{R}. \]

nodes.name: Linear systems and the q-cone
nodes.statement: Let~$D\in\mathrm{Div}^0(G)$. Then $\mathcal{K}_D$ is a rational simplicial~$n$-cone with apex~$p:=\tilde{L}^{-1}(-D|_{q=0})\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\left\{ 0 \right\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and has the following properties: \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*] \item The set of integer points of~$\mathcal{K}_D$ is in bijection with~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ via the mapping \begin{align*} \psi_D\colon\mathcal{K}_D\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}&\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb{E}_{[D]}\\ (f,k)\ &\mapsto D+kq+Lf. \end{align*} \item The mapping~$\psi_0$ restricts to a bijection between generating sets of integral extreme rays for~$\mathcal{K}_D$ and sets of primary divisors for~$G$. Let~$\Omega$ be a generating set of integral extreme rays for~$\mathcal{K}_D$ with corresponding set of primary divisors~$\mathcal{P}=\psi_0(\Omega)$. Let~$\Pi$ be the corresponding fundamental parallelepiped. Then $\psi_D$ restricts to a bijection between the integer points of~$\Pi$ and the secondary divisors of $[D]$ with respect to $\mathcal{P}$. \item Let~$\Omega$ and~$\Pi$ be as in part~\ref{poly2}. Then the~$\lambda$-sequence generating function for~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ is \[ \Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\sigma_{\mathcal{K}}(1,\dots,1,z)=\frac{\sigma_{\Pi}(1,\dots,1,z)}{\prod_{\omega\in\Omega}(1-z^{\deg(\omega)})}, \] where~$\deg(\omega)$ is the sum of the coordinates of~$\omega$. The numerator and denominator of the expression on the right are the same as those appearing in Corollary~\ref{cor: ps-genfun}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{K}_D$ is a rational simplicial cone whose lattice points biject with $\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$, extreme rays with primary divisors and parallelepiped points with secondary divisors.
conclusions: Then $\mathcal{K}_D$ is a rational simplicial~$n$-cone with apex~$p:=\tilde{L}^{-1}(-D|_{q=0})\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\left\{ 0 \right\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and has the following properties:

The set of integer points of~$\mathcal{K}_D$ is in bijection with~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ via the mapping \begin{align*} \psi_D\colon\mathcal{K}_D\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}&\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb{E}_{[D]}\\ (f,k)\ &\mapsto D+kq+Lf.
The mapping~$\psi_0$ restricts to a bijection between generating sets of integral extreme rays for~$\mathcal{K}_D$ and sets of primary divisors for~$G$.
Then $\psi_D$ restricts to a bijection between the integer points of~$\Pi$ and the secondary divisors of $[D]$ with respect to $\mathcal{P}$.

Then the~$\lambda$-sequence generating function for~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ is \[ \Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\sigma_{\mathcal{K}}(1,\dots,1,z)=\frac{\sigma_{\Pi}(1,\dots,1,z)}{\prod_{\omega\in\Omega}(1-z^{\deg(\omega)})}, \] where~$\deg(\omega)$ is the sum of the coordinates of~$\omega$.
nodes.label: thm: poly

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.4
nodes.statement: Let~$\tilde{r}_n\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ denote the last row of~$L$ with its last entry removed. Then \begin{equation} \mathcal{K}_D = \left\{ (f,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{R}: \tilde{L} f\geq -D|_{q=0}\text{ and }\tilde{r}_n\cdot f+t\geq-D(q)\right\}. \end{equation} Since~$\tilde{L}$ is invertible, these defining conditions are independent, and it follows that~$\mathcal{K}_D$ is a rational~$n$-cone. To find the apex, first solve~$\tilde{L} f=-D|_{q=0}$ to find~$f=\tilde{L}^{-1}(-D|_{q=0})$. Next, since the sum of the rows of~$L$ is~$0$, if follows that~$\tilde{r}_n\cdot f=-\tilde{L} f$, and it is now easy to verify that the last coordinate of the apex is~$t=0$ using the fact that~$\deg(D)=0$. The rest follows immediately from the discussion preceding the theorem. Part~\ref{poly1} uses the fact that every firing script has a unique representative modulo $\ker L$ having final coordinate~$0$. Part~\ref{poly2} relies on Property~\ref{property: characterization}. Part~\ref{poly3} follows since~$\deg\psi_D(f,k)=k$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $\mathcal{K}_D$ with the reduced Laplacian; invertibility gives a simplicial cone and its apex; parts follow from the preceding discussion and Property 4.1.

nodes.name: Description of the q-cone via the reduced Laplacian
nodes.statement: \mathcal{K}_D = \left\{ (f,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{R}: \tilde{L} f\geq -D|_{q=0}\text{ and }\tilde{r}_n\cdot f+t\geq-D(q)\right\}.
nodes.label: eqn: K_D

nodes.name: Bottom facet of the q-cone
nodes.statement: Given~$D\in\mathrm{Div}^0(G)$, take the union of the nested sequence of polytopes~$P_D\subset P_{D+q}\subset P_{D+2q}\subset\dots$ to define \[ \widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D:=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{N}} P_{D+kq}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n-1}. \] \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*] \item $\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D$ is a rational simplicial~$(n-1)$-cone, and \[ \widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D=\left\{ f\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}:\tilde{L} f\geq-D|_{q=0} \right\}. \] The apex of~$\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D$ is~$\tilde{p}:=\tilde{L}^{-1}(-D|_{q=0})\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$. \item Let~$\tilde{r}_n\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ be the last row of the Laplacian matrix with its final entry removed. Then there is a injection \begin{align*} \imath_D\colon\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D&\to\mathcal{K}_D\subset\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{R}\\ f&\mapsto (f,-D(q)-(\tilde{r}_n\cdot f)). \end{align*} The image of~$\imath_D$ is the facet of~$\mathcal{K}_D$ which is the intersection of~$K_D$ with the hyperplane \[ H:=\left\{(f,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{R}: (\tilde{r}_n\cdot f)+t=-D(q) \right\}, \] and \[ \mathcal{K}_D=\imath_D(\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D)+\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}q. \] \item Write \[ \widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D=\left\{\tilde{p}+\lambda_1\tilde{\omega}_1 +\dots+\lambda_{n-1}\tilde{\omega}_{n-1}: \lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{n-1}\geq0 \right\} \] with integral generating set~$\tilde{\Omega}:=\{\tilde{\omega}_1,\dots,\tilde{\omega}_{n-1}\}\subset\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$. Let~$\tilde{v}_i$ denote the~$i$-th standard basis vector for~$\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$. Then up to re-indexing, $\tilde{\omega}_i=\tilde{L}^{-1}(\ell_{i}\tilde{v}_i)$ where~$\ell_{i}$ is a positive integer multiple of~$\mathrm{ord}_q(v_i)$. The set $\Omega:=\imath_0(\tilde{\Omega})\cup\left\{ \ell_qq \right\}$ is an integral generating set of extreme rays for~$\mathcal{K}_D$ for any choice of positive integer~$\ell_q$. Every integral generating set of extreme rays for~$\mathcal{K}_D$ arises in this manner. With this notation, let~$\widetilde{\Pi}$ and~$\Pi$ be the fundamental parallelepipeds for~$\tilde{\Omega}$ and~$\Omega$, respectively. Then \[ \Pi\cap\mathbb{Z}^n=\left\{ \imath_D(\tilde{\pi})+\ell q: \tilde{\pi}\in\widetilde{\Pi}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}\text{ and } 0\leq \ell<\ell_q\right\}. \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The union of the polytopes $P_{D+kq}$ is a simplicial $(n-1)$-cone that lifts to the bottom facet of $\mathcal{K}_D$ and determines its generators and parallelepiped.
conclusions: $\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D$ is a rational simplicial~$(n-1)$-cone, and \[ \widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D=\left\{ f\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}:\tilde{L} f\geq-D|_{q=0} \right\}. \] The apex of~$\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D$ is~$\tilde{p}:=\tilde{L}^{-1}(-D|_{q=0})\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$.

Then there is a injection \begin{align*} \imath_D\colon\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D&\to\mathcal{K}_D\subset\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{R}\\ f&\mapsto (f,-D(q)-(\tilde{r}_n\cdot f)). \end{align*} The image of~$\imath_D$ is the facet of~$\mathcal{K}_D$ which is the intersection of~$K_D$ with the hyperplane \[ H:=\left\{(f,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{R}: (\tilde{r}_n\cdot f)+t=-D(q) \right\}, \] and \[ \mathcal{K}_D=\imath_D(\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D)+\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}q. \]

Then up to re-indexing, $\tilde{\omega}_i=\tilde{L}^{-1}(\ell_{i}\tilde{v}_i)$ where~$\ell_{i}$ is a positive integer multiple of~$\mathrm{ord}_q(v_i)$. The set $\Omega:=\imath_0(\tilde{\Omega})\cup\left\{ \ell_qq \right\}$ is an integral generating set of extreme rays for~$\mathcal{K}_D$ for any choice of positive integer~$\ell_q$. Every integral generating set of extreme rays for~$\mathcal{K}_D$ arises in this manner. With this notation, let~$\widetilde{\Pi}$ and~$\Pi$ be the fundamental parallelepipeds for~$\tilde{\Omega}$ and~$\Omega$, respectively. Then \[ \Pi\cap\mathbb{Z}^n=\left\{ \imath_D(\tilde{\pi})+\ell q: \tilde{\pi}\in\widetilde{\Pi}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}\text{ and } 0\leq \ell<\ell_q\right\}. \]
nodes.label: prop: facet

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.5
nodes.statement: We have~$f\in\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D$ if and only if \[ \tilde{L} f\geq-D|_{q=0}\quad\text{and}\quad \tilde{r}_n\cdot f\geq -D(q)-k \] for some~$k\in\mathbb{N}$. The second condition is superfluous since~$k$ can be arbitrarily large. The fact that~$\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}$ is a rational simplicial~$(n-1)$-cone with apex~$\tilde{L}^{-1}(-D|_{q=0})$ follows since~$\tilde{L}$ is invertible. This establishes part~\ref{facet1}. Part~\ref{facet2} then follows from part~\ref{facet1} and the description of~$\mathcal{K}_D$ given in~\eqref{eqn: K_D} in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm: poly}. Since~$K_D=\imath_D{\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}q$, part~\ref{facet3} follows from Theorem~\ref{thm: poly}~\ref{poly2} and Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}~\ref{ps-2}.
nodes.statement_short: Characterize $\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D$ by the reduced-Laplacian inequalities (the last one is superfluous), then lift using the description of $\mathcal{K}_D$ and Theorems 4.4 and 3.1.

nodes.name: Cone for D=(1,0,-1) on C_3
nodes.statement_short: On $C_3$ with $D=(1,0,-1)$: generators, apex, parallelepiped points and $\Lambda_{[D]}=(z+z^2+z^3)/((1-z^3)^2(1-z))$.
nodes.label: example: cone

nodes.name: Composition of a polynomial with a matrix
nodes.statement: Given a matrix~$A\in\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}^n)$ and a polynomial~$f\in\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]:=\mathbb{C}[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, define~$f\circ A$ by \[ (f\circ A)(x_1,\dots,x_n)=f(A\vec{x}) \] where~$\vec{x}$ is the column vector~$[x_1,\dots,x_n]^t$.

nodes.name: Relative invariants
nodes.statement: Given a finite subgroup~$\Gamma$ of~$\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}^n)$ and a character~$\chi\colon\Gamma\to\mathbb{C}^{\times}:=\mathbb{C}\setminus\left\{ 0 \right\}$, define the {\em $\chi$-relative invariants of~$\Gamma$} to be elements of \[ \mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{\chi}:=\left\{ f\in\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]: f\circ\gamma=\chi(\gamma)f \text{ for all~$\gamma\in\Gamma$} \right\}. \]

nodes.name: Relative Reynolds operator
nodes.statement: The~{\em $\chi$-relative Reynolds operator} is defined for each polynomial~$f\in\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]$ by \[ \mathcal{R}_{\chi}(f)=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\overline{\chi}(\gamma)f\circ\gamma. \]

nodes.name: Reynolds operator characterizes relative invariants
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that~$\mathcal{R}_{\chi}$ is linear in~$f$ and that~$f$ is~$\chi$-invariant if and only if~$\mathcal{R}_{\chi}(f)=f$.
conclusions: $\mathcal{R}_{\chi}$ is linear in~$f$
$f$ is~$\chi$-invariant if and only if~$\mathcal{R}_{\chi}(f)=f$

nodes.name: Invariant subring
nodes.statement: In the case~$\chi=\varepsilon$, the trivial character, $\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}:=\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{\varepsilon}$ is a subring of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]$, graded by degree, called the {\em invariant subring of~$\Gamma$}.

nodes.name: Invariants and Reynolds operator
nodes.statement: The elements of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}$ are simply called~{\em invariants of~$\Gamma$} and~$\mathcal{R}:=\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}$ is the~{\em Reynolds operator for~$\Gamma$}.

nodes.name: Existence of primary invariants
nodes.statement: There exist algebraically independent homogeneous invariants~$p_1,\dots,p_n$ such that~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}$ is a finitely-generated free module over $\mathbb{C}[p_1,\dots,p_n]$.
conclusions: There exist algebraically independent homogeneous invariants~$p_1,\dots,p_n$ such that~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}$ is a finitely-generated free module over $\mathbb{C}[p_1,\dots,p_n]$

nodes.name: Hironaka decomposition of relative invariants
nodes.statement: For any character~$\chi$, if~$q_1,\dots,q_t$ are homogeneous polynomials forming a~$\mathbb{C}$-basis for~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{\chi}$ modulo the submodule $\sum_{i=1}^np_i\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{\chi}$, then \[ \mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]_{\chi}^{\Gamma}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{t}q_i\mathbb{C}[p_1,\dots,p_n]. \]
assumptions: if~$q_1,\dots,q_t$ are homogeneous polynomials forming a~$\mathbb{C}$-basis for~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{\chi}$ modulo the submodule $\sum_{i=1}^np_i\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{\chi}$
conclusions: \mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]_{\chi}^{\Gamma}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{t}q_i\mathbb{C}[p_1,\dots,p_n].

nodes.name: Primary invariants
nodes.statement: The~$p_i$ are called {\em primary invariants} and are independent of~$\chi$.

nodes.name: Secondary invariants
nodes.statement: The~$q_i$ are called {\em secondary (relative) invariants} and depend on~$\chi$.

nodes.name: Number of secondary invariants
nodes.statement: However, letting~$t_{\varepsilon}$ be the number of secondary invariants for the trivial character, we have \[ t_{\varepsilon}|\Gamma|=\prod_{i=1}^n\deg(p_i). \]
conclusions: t_{\varepsilon}|\Gamma|=\prod_{i=1}^n\deg(p_i).

nodes.name: Hilbert series
nodes.statement: The {\em Hilbert series} for~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{\chi}$ is \[ \Phi_{\Gamma,\chi}(z):=\sum_{d\geq 0}\dim_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]_{\chi,d}^{\Gamma})z^d, \] where~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]_{\chi,d}^{\Gamma}$ denotes the~$d$-th graded piece of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]_{\chi}^{\Gamma}$.

nodes.name: Molien series
nodes.statement: The Hilbert series is also known as the (relative) {\em Molien series} for~$\Gamma$ due to a theorem of Molien which states that \begin{equation} \Phi_{\Gamma,\chi}(z) = \frac{1}{|\Gamma|}\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\frac{\overline{\chi(\gamma)}}{\det(I_n-z\gamma)}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Molien's theorem
nodes.statement: \Phi_{\Gamma,\chi}(z) = \frac{1}{|\Gamma|}\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\frac{\overline{\chi(\gamma)}}{\det(I_n-z\gamma)}.
conclusions: \Phi_{\Gamma,\chi}(z) = \frac{1}{|\Gamma|}\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\frac{\overline{\chi(\gamma)}}{\det(I_n-z\gamma)}.
nodes.label: eqn: Molien

nodes.name: Representation rho of the dual Jacobian
nodes.statement: Define~$\rho$ to be the composition of these mappings: \begin{align} \rho\colon\mathrm{Jac}(G)^{*}\ &\xrightarrow{\qquad}\qquad\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}^n)\\ \nonumber \chi\qquad &\mapsto\quad\mathrm{diag}(\chi([v_1-q]),\chi([v_2-q]),\dots,\chi([v_{n-1}-q]),1). \end{align}

nodes.name: Representation rho
nodes.statement: \rho\colon\mathrm{Jac}(G)^{*}\ &\xrightarrow{\qquad}\qquad\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}^n)\\ \nonumber \chi\qquad &\mapsto\quad\mathrm{diag}(\chi([v_1-q]),\chi([v_2-q]),\dots,\chi([v_{n-1}-q]),1).
nodes.label: rho

nodes.name: Linear systems as relative invariants
nodes.statement: Consider each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ as a character of~$\Gamma:=\mathrm{im}(\rho)\subset\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}^n)$ via~$[D](\rho(\chi)):=\chi([D])$ for each~$\chi\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)^{*}$. Then \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*] \item \[ \textstyle \left\{x^{E}:=\prod_{i=1}^nx_i^{E(v_i)}: E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]} \right\} \] is a~$\mathbb{C}$-basis for the relative invariants~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{[D]}$, \item $\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]=\bigoplus_{[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)}\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{[D]}$, and \item the correspondence~$E\mapsto x^{E}$ for effective divisors~$E$ gives a bijection between systems of primary and~$[D]$-secondary divisors and systems of monomial primary and~$[D]$-relative invariants. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Monomials $x^E$, $E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$, form a basis of the $[D]$-relative invariants of $\mathrm{im}(\rho)$; primary/secondary divisors correspond to monomial primary/secondary invariants.
assumptions: Consider each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ as a character of~$\Gamma:=\mathrm{im}(\rho)\subset\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}^n)$ via~$[D](\rho(\chi)):=\chi([D])$ for each~$\chi\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)^{*}$.
conclusions: \textstyle \left\{x^{E}:=\prod_{i=1}^nx_i^{E(v_i)}: E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]} \right\} \] is a~$\mathbb{C}$-basis for the relative invariants~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{[D]}$
$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]=\bigoplus_{[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)}\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{[D]}$
the correspondence~$E\mapsto x^{E}$ for effective divisors~$E$ gives a bijection between systems of primary and~$[D]$-secondary divisors and systems of monomial primary and~$[D]$-relative invariants.
nodes.label: thm: invariants

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.1
nodes.statement: An arbitrary element of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]$ may be written as~$f=\sum^{\,}_{E}a_Ex^E$ where the sum is over all effective divisors of~$G$ and all but finitely many~$a_E$ are zero. Let~$\chi\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)^{*}$. Then \allowdisplaybreaks \begin{align*} f\circ\rho(\chi) &= \sum_{E}a^{\,}_E(x^E\circ\rho(\chi))\\ &= \sum_{E}a^{\,}_E\textstyle\left(\prod_{v\in V}\chi([v-q])^{E(v)} \right)x^E\\ &= \sum_{E}a^{\,}_E\textstyle\,\chi\!\left(\sum_{v\in V}E(v)([v-q])\right)x^E\\ &= \sum_{E}a^{\,}_E\textstyle\,\chi\!\left([E-\deg(E)q]\right)x^E. \end{align*} Therefore,~$f\in\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{[D]}$ if and only if for each~$E$ such that~$a^{\,}_E\neq0$, we have $\chi([E-\deg(E)q])=\chi([D])$ for all~$\chi$, or equivalently, $[E-\deg(E)q]=[D]$, i.e.,~$E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$. Parts~\ref{inv1},~\ref{inv2}, and~\ref{inv3} follow. Part~\ref{inv2} reflects the fact that the~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ partition the set of effective divisors.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the action of $\rho(\chi)$ on monomials: $x^E$ is scaled by $\chi([E-\deg(E)q])$, so $[D]$-invariance means $E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.2
nodes.statement: As an immediate corollary, we may express $\lambda$-sequence generating functions as a Molien series.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from Theorem 5.1 and Molien's theorem.

nodes.name: Molien series for the lambda-sequence
nodes.statement: Let~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$. The generating function for the $\lambda$-sequence for~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ is given by the Molien series \[ \Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\Phi_{\Gamma,[D]}(z) =\frac{1}{|\mathrm{Jac}(G)|}\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)^{*}}\frac{\overline{\chi([D])}}{\det(I_n-z\rho(\chi))}. \]
nodes.statement_short: $\Lambda_{[D]}(z)$ is the relative Molien series: an average over characters of $\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ of $\overline{\chi([D])}/\det(I-z\rho(\chi))$.
conclusions: The generating function for the $\lambda$-sequence for~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ is given by the Molien series \[ \Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\Phi_{\Gamma,[D]}(z) =\frac{1}{|\mathrm{Jac}(G)|}\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)^{*}}\frac{\overline{\chi([D])}}{\det(I_n-z\rho(\chi))}. \]
nodes.label: cor: lambda-molien

nodes.name: Computing the Molien series via Smith normal form
nodes.statement: To compute with Corollary~\ref{cor: lambda-molien} concretely, use integer row and column operations to reduce~$\tilde{L}$ to diagonal form (e.g., Smith normal form), denoting the result by~$M:=\mathrm{diag}(m_1,\dots,m_{n-1})$. Record the row and column operations in matrices~$U$ and~$W$ so that~$U\tilde{L} W = M$. Then~$U$ descends to an isomorphism \[ \mathrm{Jac}(G)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}/\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}\xrightarrow{\ U\ }\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\mathbb{Z}/m_i\mathbb{Z}. \] Having identified~$\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ with~$R:=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\mathbb{Z}/m_i\mathbb{Z}$, we now describe the characters. For each~$r\in R$, choose a representative lifting~$(r_1,\dots,r_{n-1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$, and let $ \tilde{r} := \left(\frac{r_1}{m_1},\dots,\frac{r_{n-1}}{m_{n-1}} \right)$. Define the character~$\tilde{\chi}_r\in R^*$ by \[ \tilde{\chi}_r(a) :=\exp(2\pi i\,(\tilde{r}\cdot a)) \] for each~$a\in R$. Then define~$\chi_r\in\mathrm{Jac}^*(G)$ by \[ \chi_r([D]):=\tilde{\chi}_r(U(D|_{q=0})) \] for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$. It follows that \[ \rho(\chi_r)=\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{\chi}_r(u_1),\tilde{\chi}_r(u_2),\dots,\tilde{\chi}_r(u_{n-1}),1) \] where~$u_j$ is the~$j$-th column of~$U$. In all of the above, if~$m_k=1$ for some~$k$, then the~$k$-th factor of~$R$ and the~$k$-th {\em row} of~$U$ may be dropped.
nodes.statement_short: Diagonalize $\tilde{L}$ (Smith normal form) to identify $\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ with a product of cyclic groups, then write characters and $\rho(\chi_r)$ explicitly.

nodes.name: Trees (Molien)
nodes.statement: If~$G$ is a tree, then~$\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ is trivial, and~$\mathrm{Jac}(G)^*$ contains only the trivial character. So Corollary~\ref{cor: lambda-molien} says~$\Lambda_{[0](z)}=1/(1-z)^{n}$.

nodes.name: Diamond graph (Molien)
nodes.statement: Now let~$G$ be the diamond graph of Figure~\ref{fig: diamond graph}. Letting \[ U = \left(\begin{array}{rrr} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & -4 \end{array}\right) \quad\text{and}\quad W = \left(\begin{array}{rrr} 3 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 4 \end{array}\right), \] we have~$U\tilde{L} W =\mathrm{diag}(1,1,8)$ and the corresponding isomorphism \begin{align*} \mathrm{Jac}(G)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{3}/\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}&\to\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}\\ (a,b,c)&\mapsto a-b-4c. \end{align*} The divisor class~$[v_1-q]$ generates~$\mathrm{Jac}(G)$. Let~$D_j=j[v_1-q]$ for~$j=0,\dots,7$, and let $\omega=\exp(2\pi i/8)$. Then, by Corollary~\ref{cor: lambda-molien}, \[ \Lambda_{[D_j]} = \frac{1}{8(1-z)}\sum_{k=0}^7\frac{\omega^{-jk}}{(1-\omega^{k}z)(1-\omega^{-k}z)(1-\omega^{-4k}z)} \] for~$j=0,\dots,7$.
nodes.statement_short: Diamond graph: Smith normal form $\mathrm{diag}(1,1,8)$ gives $\Lambda_{[D_j]}$ as an average over eighth roots of unity.

nodes.name: Cycle graphs (Molien)
nodes.statement: Now let~$G=C_n$ be a cycle graph using the notation of Example~\ref{example: ps-cycle}. Let~$I_n$ be the~$n\times n$ identity matrix, and let~$U$ be the matrix formed by replacing the last row of the~$-I_n$ with the row $(1,2,\dots,(n-2),-1)$. Let~$W$ be the~$n\times n$ matrix with $W_{ij}=-\min\left\{ i,j \right\}$ (so~$W$ starts with a row of~$-1$s and ends with the row $(-1,-2,\dots,-(n-1))$). Then~$U\tilde{L} W=\mathrm{diag}(1,1,\dots,1,n)$, and multiplication by~$U$ gives the isomorphism \begin{align*} \mathrm{Jac}(C_n)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}/\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}&\to\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\\ (a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})&\mapsto a_1+2a_2+\dots+(n-2)a_{n-2}+(n-1)a_{n-1}. \end{align*} The divisor class~$[v_{1}-q]$ generates~$\mathrm{Jac}(C_n)$. Let $D_j=j[v_{1}-q]$ for~$j=0,\dots,n-1$, and let~$\omega=\exp(2\pi i/n)$. Then by Corollary~\ref{cor: lambda-molien}, \[ \Lambda_{[D_j]}(z) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{\omega^{-jk}}{\prod_{t=0}^{n-1}(1-\omega^{tk}z)} \] for~$j=0,\dots,n-1$. In particular, \[ \Lambda_{[0]}(z)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(1-z^{n/\gcd(n,k)})^{\gcd(n,k)}} =\frac{1}{n}\sum_{d|n}\frac{\phi(d)}{(1-z^d)^{n/d}} \] where~$\phi$ is the Euler totient function. We shall explore this example further in Section~\ref{sect: necklaces}.
nodes.statement_short: Cycle graph: $\Lambda_{[D_j]}$ as an average over $n$-th roots of unity; $\Lambda_{[0]}=\frac1n\sum_{d|n}\phi(d)/(1-z^d)^{n/d}$.

nodes.name: Complete graphs (Molien)
nodes.statement: Let~$G=K_n$. Perform integer column operations to bring~$\tilde{L}$ into Hermite normal form~$H$ as described in Example~\ref{example: ps-complete}. Next, let~$U$ be the matrix formed by replacing the first column of the identity matrix~$I_{n-1}$ by the column $(1,-1,-1,\dots,-1)$. Then~$UH = M:=\mathrm{diag}(1,n,n,\dots,n)$. Since~$M_{1,1}=1$, alter~$U$ by removing its first row, and we get an isomorphism \[ \mathrm{Jac}(K_n)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}/\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}\xrightarrow{U}R:=\left(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \right)^{n-2}. \] Let~$\omega:=\exp(2\pi i/n)$. Then for each~$r\in R$, we have the character~$\chi_r$ such that~$\chi_r(a)=\omega^{r\cdot a}$ for each $a\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}/\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}$. By Corollary~\ref{cor: lambda-molien}, for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, writing~$D=(d_1,\dots,d_n)$, \[ \Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\frac{1}{n^{n-2}(1-z)}\sum_{r\in (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{n-2}}\frac{\omega^{-r\cdot(d_2-d_1,\dots,d_{n-1}-d_1)}}{(1-\omega^{-r_1-\dots-r_{n-2}}z)(1-\omega^{r_1}z)(1-\omega^{r_2}z)\dots(1-\omega^{r_{n-2}}z)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Complete graph: $\mathrm{Jac}(K_n)\simeq(\mathbb{Z}/n)^{n-2}$ and an explicit Molien-type sum with $n^{n-2}$ terms.

nodes.name: Comparing the two generating function formulas
nodes.statement: Corollaries~\ref{cor: ps-genfun} and~\ref{cor: lambda-molien} give two ways of expressing the generating function~$\Lambda_{[D]}(z)$. One sums over elements of~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$, and the other sums over elements of~$\mathrm{Jac}^*(G)$. In practice, one of these two expressions may be much simpler than the other. For instance, the complete graph~$K_n$ has a large Jacobian group,~$|\mathrm{Jac}(K_n)|=n^{n-2}$, however we can find a set of secondary divisors with only~$n$ elements. So the expression for~$\Lambda_{[D]}(z)$ coming from Corollary~\ref{cor: lambda-molien} will have~$n^{n-2}$ summands while the numerator~$S$ appearing in Corollary~\ref{cor: ps-genfun} with have only~$n$ terms. In the case of the cyclic graph~$C_n$, we have the opposite situation:~$|\mathrm{Jac}(C_n)|=n$ and there are~$n^{n-2}$ secondary divisors (taking~$\ell_v=n$ for all vertices~$v\neq 1$).
nodes.statement_short: The secondary-divisor formula is short for $K_n$ ($n$ terms vs $n^{n-2}$), while the Molien formula is short for $C_n$.

nodes.name: Colors and words
nodes.statement: Let~$C$ be a finite set of~{\em colors} and let~$C^n$ denote the set of all words (strings) of length~$n$ with letters in~$C$.

nodes.name: Cyclic shift operator
nodes.statement: Let~$\sigma$ be the cyclic shift operator on~$C^n$: \[ \sigma(c_1\dots c_n) = c_n c_1\dots c_{n-1}. \]

nodes.name: Rotation equivalence of words
nodes.statement: Define an equivalence relation on~$C^n$ by letting~$w\sim w'$ if~$w=\sigma^i(w')$ for some integer~$i$.

nodes.name: Necklace
nodes.statement: A {\em necklace} of length~$n$ on the color set~$C$ is an equivalence class $[c_1\dots c_n]\in C^n/\!\!\sim$.

nodes.name: Period of a necklace
nodes.statement: The~{\em period} of a necklace~$N=[w]$ is the smallest positive integer~$i$ such that~$\sigma^i(w)=w$.

nodes.name: m-divisible necklace
nodes.statement: Let~$m$ be a positive integer. A necklace is {\em $m$-divisible} if its period is divisible by~$m$. (See Figure~\ref{fig: necklaces} for an example.)

nodes.name: Binary necklace
nodes.statement: A {\em binary necklace} is a necklace for which~$C$ consists of two colors (which we take to be black and white).

nodes.name: Code of a binary necklace
nodes.statement: Let~$N=[bw^{a_1}bw^{a_2}\cdots bw^{a_n}]\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$. The {\em code} for~$N$ is the necklace with~$n$ beads and with colors~$\left\{ a_1,\dots,a_n \right\}\subset\mathbb{N}$, \[ \mathrm{code}(N):=[a_1\dots a_n]. \]

nodes.name: Cycle graph C_n
nodes.statement: Let~$C_n$ be the cycle graph with vertices $v_1,\dots,v_n$ around the cycle, and take~$q:=v_n$.

nodes.name: Divisors D_i on C_n
nodes.statement: Working with subscripts modulo~$n$, let~$D_i=v_i-q\in\mathrm{Div}(C_n)$ for all~$i\in\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.name: Generator chi_1 of the dual group
nodes.statement: The dual group~$\mathrm{Jac}(C_n)^*$ is generated by the character~$\chi_1$ determined by $\chi_1([D_1])=\omega$ where~$\omega$ is a primitive~$n$-th root of unity.

nodes.name: Vectors v(x) and Vandermonde-type matrix A
nodes.statement: In detail, for any~$x\in\mathbb{C}$, let~$v(x):=(x,x^2,\dots,x^n)$ and let~$A$ be the matrix with rows $v(\omega^n),v(\omega),v(\omega^{2}),\dots,v(\omega^{n-1})$.

nodes.name: Permutation representation rho'
nodes.statement: Conjugate by~$A$ to get~$\rho':\mathrm{Jac}(G)^*\to\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}^n)$ where $\rho'(\chi)=A\rho(\chi)A^{-1}$ for all~$\chi\in\mathrm{Jac}^*(C_n)$.

nodes.name: rho'(chi_1) is a cyclic permutation matrix
nodes.statement: Then~$\rho'(\chi_1)$ is the permutation matrix~$P$ such that for each standard basis vector~$e_1,\dots,e_n$, we have~$Pe_i=e_{i-1}$ (with subscripts modulo~$n$).
conclusions: $\rho'(\chi_1)$ is the permutation matrix~$P$ such that for each standard basis vector~$e_1,\dots,e_n$, we have~$Pe_i=e_{i-1}$

nodes.name: Groups Gamma, Gamma' and indeterminates y
nodes.statement: Let~$\Gamma=\mathrm{im}(\rho)$ and~$\Gamma':=\mathrm{im}(\rho')$, and define indeterminates~$y=Ax$.

nodes.name: Isomorphism of relative invariant rings
nodes.statement: It follows that for each~$[D_j]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ (considered as a character on~$\mathrm{Jac}(G)^*$), there is an induced, degree-preserving, linear isomorphism of relative invariant rings \begin{align} \mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j]}&\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{[D_j]}\\\nonumber f\quad&\mapsto f\circ A. \end{align}
conclusions: there is an induced, degree-preserving, linear isomorphism of relative invariant rings

nodes.name: Isomorphism between permutation and diagonal relative invariants
nodes.statement: \mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j]}&\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{[D_j]}\\\nonumber f\quad&\mapsto f\circ A.
nodes.label: eqn: permutation iso

nodes.name: Invariants f_N from necklaces
nodes.statement: For each $N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$, fix a representative word~$a_N$ for the necklace~$\mathrm{code}(N)$, and use the Reynolds operator to define \[ f_N(y):=\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^{a_N})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\omega^{-ij}y^{\sigma^i(a_N)}, \] where~$\sigma$ is the cyclic shift operator defined earlier and~$y^{a_N}:=\prod_{i=1}^ny_i^{a_{N,i}}$.

nodes.name: Necklace basis for relative invariants
nodes.statement: Let~$j\in[n]$ and define \[ m_j:=\frac{n+k}{\gcd(n,k,j)}\quad\text{and}\quad n_j:=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,j)}=\mathrm{order}(\omega^j). \] \begin{enumerate}[label=\rm{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*] \item $N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ is~$m_j$-divisible if and only if~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n_j$-divisible. \item The set $\left\{ f_N \right\}$ as~$N$ ranges over all~$m_j$-divisible~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ is a basis for the~$[D_j]$-relative invariants of degree~$k$ for the permutation representation~$\rho'$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $N$ is $m_j$-divisible iff its code is $n_j$-divisible, and the Reynolds images $f_N$ of $m_j$-divisible necklaces form a basis of degree-$k$ $[D_j]$-relative invariants.
conclusions: $N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ is~$m_j$-divisible if and only if~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n_j$-divisible.
The set $\left\{ f_N \right\}$ as~$N$ ranges over all~$m_j$-divisible~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ is a basis for the~$[D_j]$-relative invariants of degree~$k$ for the permutation representation~$\rho'$.
nodes.label: thm: permutation invariants

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.3
nodes.statement:
Let~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$, and let~$a=a_N=a_1\dots a_n$ be a representative word for $\mathrm{code}(N)$. We first show that~$N$ is~$m_j$-divisible if and only if~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n_j$-divisible. Let~$\ell$ be the period of~$\mathrm{code}(N)$. Then since the length of the necklace~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n$, there is an integer~$p$ such that~$n=p\ell$. The period of~$N$ is~$\ell+\alpha$ where~$\alpha:=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}a_i$. Since~$\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i=k$, and the period of~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$\ell$, it follows that~$p\alpha=k$. Therefore,  egin{align*} 	ext{$N$ is~$m_j$-divisible}&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \left(  rac{n+k}{\gcd(n,k,j)}ight) igg|\,(\ell+\alpha)\[8pt] &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad rac{p(\ell+\alpha)}{\gcd(p\ell,p\alpha,j)} igg|\,(\ell+\alpha)\[8pt] &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad  rac{\gcd(p\ell,p\alpha,j)}{p(\ell+\alpha)}\cdot(\ell+\alpha)\in\mathbb{Z}\[8pt] &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p|j. \end{align*} Similarly, \[ 	ext{$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n_j$-divisible} \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad\left(  rac{n}{\gcd(n,j)} ight) igg|\,\ell \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad rac{p\ell}{\gcd(p\ell,j)} igg|\,\ell \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad p|j. \] Continuing with the notation already established, we now prove part~ef{basis part2}. Since~$f_N$ is defined using the Reynolds operator, it is~$[D_j]$-invariant. To see that it is non-zero, we show that the monomial~$y^a$ appears in~$f_N$ with a nonzero coefficient. We have~$y^a=y^{\sigma^i(a)}$ if and only if~$i$ is a multiple of the period~$\ell$. However,~$\ell$ is divisible by~$n_j$, which is the order of~$\omega^{j}$. So the coefficient of~$y^{\sigma^i(a)}$ in the expression for the Reynolds operator is~$\omega^{-ij}/n=1/n$. Therefore, the coefficient of~$y^{a}$ in~$f_N$ is the integer~$p/n=1/\ell
eq0$. It now follows that~$f_N$ has degree~$k$. Let~$\mathcal{B}$ be the set of~$f_N$ as~$N$ varies over~$m_j$-divisible elements of~$\mathcal{N}(n,k)$. Distinct elements of~$\mathcal{B}$ share no monomials in common, and hence~$\mathcal{B}$ is a linearly independent set. To show~$\mathcal{B}$ spans the relative invariant module and finish the proof, let~$h\in\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$ be a homogeneous~$[D_j]$-invariant of degree~$k$. For the sake of contradiction, suppose~$h
otin\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})$. We regard~$h$ as a sum of terms where each term is a nonzero constant times a monomial, and the monomials are distinct. Among all elements of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$ that are not in~$\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})$, let~$h$ be one with the fewest number of terms, and let~~$ eta y^b$ be one of these terms. Then~$ eta\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b)$ is a sum of terms appearing in~$h$. Let~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ be the necklace with~$\mathrm{code}(N)=[b]$. Say~$[b]$ has period~$m$ and write~$n=mq$ for some integer~$q$. The coefficient of~$y^b$ in~$\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b)$ is \[  rac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^q(\omega^{-jm})^i, \] and the order of~$\omega^{-jm}$ is~$q/\gcd(q,j)$, a divisor of~$q$. If~$[b]$ is not~$n_j$-divisible, then the order of~$\omega^j$ does not divide~$m$, and hence,~$\omega^{jm}
eq1$. It would then follow that the above sum is~$0$, which contradicts the fact that~$ eta y^b$ is a term of~$h$. Therefore,~$[b]$ is~$n_j$-divisible and~$\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b)=f_N\in\mathcal{B}$. However, then the polynomial~$h- eta f_N$ is an element of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$ with fewer terms than~$h$ and not in~$\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})$, which is a contradiction. So~$\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})=\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Divisibility equivalence by comparing periods of $N$ and its code; basis by showing $f_N\neq 0$ and a minimal-counterexample spanning argument.

nodes.name: Linear systems on cycles count divisible necklaces
nodes.statement: With notation as in the theorem, \begin{align*} \#|D_j+kq|&= \#\left\{ N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k):\text{$N$ is~$m_j$-divisible} \right\}\\[5pt] &= \#\left\{ N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k):\text{$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n_j$-divisible} \right\}. \end{align*} In particular,~$\#|kq|=\#\mathcal{N}(n,k)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\#|D_j+kq|$ equals the number of $m_j$-divisible binary necklaces in $\mathcal{N}(n,k)$; in particular $\#|kq|=\#\mathcal{N}(n,k)$.
assumptions: With notation as in the theorem,
conclusions: \#|D_j+kq|&= \#\left\{ N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k):\text{$N$ is~$m_j$-divisible} \right\}\\[5pt] &= \#\left\{ N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k):\text{$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n_j$-divisible} \right\}.
In particular,~$\#|kq|=\#\mathcal{N}(n,k)$.
nodes.label: cor: permutation invariants

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 6.4
nodes.statement: The result follows immediately from Corollary~\ref{cor: lambda-molien}, Theorem~\ref{thm: permutation invariants}, and the degree-preserving isomorphism~(\ref{eqn: permutation iso}).
nodes.statement_short: Combine the Molien corollary, Theorem 6.3 and the degree-preserving isomorphism (7).

nodes.name: Necklaces for (n,k,j)=(4,2,1) and (4,2,2)
nodes.statement_short: Computes $m_j$, $n_j$ and the bases $f_N$ for $\mathcal{N}(4,2)$, matching the monomial bases from $|D_1+2q|$ and $|D_2+2q|$.

nodes.name: Dot product of a divisor and a vector
nodes.statement: Given~$D\in\mathrm{Div}(C_n)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^n$ and~$v\in\mathbb{Z}^n$, let~$D\cdot v$ be the usual dot product of vectors.

nodes.name: Rotation of divisors
nodes.statement: Extend the rotation operator~$\sigma$ on words to divisors by letting~$\sigma(D)(v_i):=D(v_{i+1})$ for all~$i$ modulo~$n$.

nodes.name: Linear equivalence classes on C_n
nodes.statement: Let~$n,k\in\mathbb{Z}$ with~$n>1$, and let~$D\in\mathrm{Div}(C_n)$. Let \[ \eta := (1,2,\dots,n)\quad\text{and}\quad\vec{1}=(1,1,\dots,1)\in\mathbb{Z}^n. \] Then~$D\sim D_j+kq$ if and only~$D\cdot\vec{1}=k$ and~$D\cdot\eta=j\bmod n$.
conclusions: $D\sim D_j+kq$ if and only~$D\cdot\vec{1}=k$ and~$D\cdot\eta=j\bmod n$
nodes.label: lemma: divisors on C_n

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.6
nodes.statement: First note that if~$c$ is a column of the Laplacian matrix for~$C_n$, then~$c\cdot\eta=0\bmod n$. Given any~$D\in\mathrm{Div}(C_n)$, there exists~$i$ and~$m$ such that~$D\sim D_i+mq$. Then~$D\cdot\vec{1}=m$, and \[ D\cdot\eta = (D_i+mq)\cdot\eta\bmod n= i\bmod n. \] The result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Columns of the Laplacian are orthogonal to $\eta$ mod $n$, so $D\cdot\eta$ mod $n$ and $D\cdot\vec1$ detect the class $D_i+mq$.

nodes.name: Bijection between linear systems on C_n and binary necklaces
nodes.statement: Given an effective divisor~$E=(E(v_1),\dots,E(v_n))\in\mathbb{N}^n\subset\mathrm{Div}^k(C_n)$, define the word \[ w_E:=bw^{E(v_1)}bw^{E(v_2)}\dots bw^{E(v_n)}, \] and the corresponding necklace~$N_E:=[w_E]\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ with~$\mathrm{code}(N_E)=[E(v_1)\dots E(v_n)]$. If $\gcd(n,k)=1$, then for each~$j\in[n]$, \begin{align*} \psi\colon |D_j+kq|&\to\mathcal{N}(n,k)\\ E&\mapsto N_E \end{align*} is a bijection.
nodes.statement_short: When $\gcd(n,k)=1$, $E\mapsto N_E$ is a bijection from $|D_j+kq|$ on $C_n$ to binary necklaces with $n$ black and $k$ white beads.
assumptions: Given an effective divisor~$E=(E(v_1),\dots,E(v_n))\in\mathbb{N}^n\subset\mathrm{Div}^k(C_n)$, define the word \[ w_E:=bw^{E(v_1)}bw^{E(v_2)}\dots bw^{E(v_n)}, \] and the corresponding necklace~$N_E:=[w_E]\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ with~$\mathrm{code}(N_E)=[E(v_1)\dots E(v_n)]$.
conclusions: \psi\colon |D_j+kq|&\to\mathcal{N}(n,k)\\ E&\mapsto N_E \end{align*} is a bijection.
nodes.label: thm: necklace bijection

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.7
nodes.statement: Let~$\eta=(1,2,\dots,n)$ as in Lemma~\ref{lemma: divisors on C_n}. To show injectivity, suppose~$\psi(E)=\psi(E')$ for some pair of effective divisors~$E,E'\in\mathrm{Div}^k(C_n)$. It follows that~$E'=\sigma^i(E)$ for some~$i$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma: divisors on C_n}, working modulo~$n$, \[ j = E'\cdot\eta =\sigma^i(E)\cdot\eta=E\cdot(\eta+i\vec{1})=j+ik\bmod n. \] If~$\gcd(n,k)=1$, it follows that~$i=0\bmod n$, and hence~$E=E'$. For surjectivity, let~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ with~$\mathrm{code}(N)=[a_1\dots a_n]$. Let~$E:=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathrm{Div}^k(C_n)$, and say~$E\cdot\eta=m\bmod n$. Then $\sigma^i(E)\cdot\eta=m+ik\bmod n$ for each~$i$. If~$\gcd(n,k)=1$, we can take~$i$ so that~$m+ik=j\bmod n$ and define~$E':=\sigma^i(E)$. Then~$E'\in|D_j+kq|$ and~$\psi(E')=N$.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity: equal necklaces differ by rotation, and Lemma 6.6 forces the rotation to be trivial; surjectivity: rotate the code divisor into the right class.

nodes.name: Periods and commutative diagram when gcd(n,k)=1
nodes.statement: If~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ and~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ has period~$\ell$, then as we saw in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm: permutation invariants}, both~$\ell|n$ and~$\ell|k$. Thus, if~$\gcd(n,k)=1$, it follows that~$\ell=1$. In other words, each element of~$\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ has period~$n+k$. Further, by the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm: necklace bijection}, there is a commutative diagram of isomorphisms of sets: \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} {|kq|}\arrow[d,"\sigma^j"',pos=0.35]\arrow[r,"\psi"] & \mathcal{N}(n,k)\\ {|D_j+kq|}\arrow[ru,"\psi"',pos=0.45]& \end{tikzcd}. \end{center}
nodes.statement_short: If $\gcd(n,k)=1$ every necklace in $\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ has period $n+k$, and rotation $\sigma^j$ intertwines the bijections.

nodes.name: Duality between C_n and C_k
nodes.statement: (Duality) Switching colors gives a bijection between~$\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ and~$\mathcal{N}(k,n)$. Therefore, fixing vertices~$q$ on~$C_n$ and~$q'$ on~$C_k$, Corollary~\ref{cor: permutation invariants} says that the cardinality of $|kq|$ on~$C_n$ is equal to that of ~$|nq'|$ on~$C_k$. Further, when~$n$ and~$k$ are relatively prime, Theorem~\ref{thm: necklace bijection} gives a combinatorial bijection between these complete linear systems.
nodes.statement_short: Swapping colors shows $\#|kq|$ on $C_n$ equals $\#|nq'|$ on $C_k$, bijectively when $\gcd(n,k)=1$.
