nodes.name: Entrywise order on matrices
nodes.statement: To establish notation: if~$H$ and~$H'$ are matrices or vectors of the same dimensions, write~$H\geq H'$ (resp.,~$H>H'$) if each entry of~$H-H'$ is nonnegative (resp., positive).

nodes.name: Non-singular M-matrix
nodes.statement: Let~$A$ be an~$(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrix over~$\mathbb{R}$ with~$A_{ij}\leq 0$ for all~$i\neq j$. Then~$A$ is a (non-singular)~{\em $M$-matrix} if any of the following equivalent conditions holds: \begin{enumerate} \item $A=sI_{n-1}-B$ for some matrix~$B\geq0$ and some $s>\max\left\{ |\lambda|:\text{$\lambda$ an eigenvalue of~$B$}\right\}$. \item Each eigenvalue of~$A$ has positive real part. \item Each principal minor of~$A$ is positive. \item $A^{-1}$ exists and~$A^{-1}\geq0$. \item If~$Au\geq0$, then~$u\geq0$. \item There exists~$u>0$ such that~$Au>0$. \item There exists~$u>0$ with~$Au\geq0$ and such that if~$(Au)_{i_0}=0$ for some~$i_0$, then there exists indices~$i_1,\dots,i_r$ with~$A_{i_{k}i_{k+1}}\neq0$ for~$k=1,\dots,r-1$ and~$(Au)_{i_r}>0$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A Z-matrix (nonpositive off-diagonal) is a non-singular $M$-matrix if it satisfies any of seven equivalent conditions (positive principal minors, nonnegative inverse, burning vector, ...).

nodes.name: Integer M-matrix
nodes.statement: From now on, we assume that~$A$ is an integer~$M$-matrix.

nodes.name: Burning script
nodes.statement: In that case, any integer vector~$u$ satisfying property~(\ref{item: burning}) is called a~{\em burning script}.

nodes.name: Minimal burning script construction
nodes.statement: A burning script for~$A$ always exists and a unique minimal one (with respect to~$\leq$) can be constructed as follows: start with~$u=(1,\dots,1)$, and then as long as~$(Au)_i<0$ for some~$i$, increase~$u_i$ by~$1$ (\cite{PPW}; \cite{Corry}, Chapter~7).
nodes.origin_citation: Postnikov & Shapiro & Perkinson/Perlman/Wilmes (PPW); Corry & Perkinson Ch. 7
nodes.statement_short: Start from the all-ones vector and repeatedly increment any coordinate where $Au$ is negative.
output: a unique minimal one (with respect to~$\leq$)

nodes.name: Burning configuration
nodes.statement: If~$u$ is a burning script, then~$Au$ is called a {\em burning configuration}.

nodes.name: (w,u)-extension of an M-matrix
nodes.statement: Let~$u=(u_1,\dots,u_n)>0$ and~$w=(w_1,\dots w_n)>0$ be any integer vectors such that both~$Au\geq0$ and~$wA\geq0$. Their existence is guaranteed by property~(\ref{item: burning}) and the fact that the transpose~$A^t$ of~$A$ is also an~$M$-matrix. We do not require that~$u$ and~$w$ be burning scripts. Next, define the {\em $(w,u)$-extension} of~$A$ to be the~$n\times n$ matrix \[ \widehat{A}:= \left(\begin{array}{c|c} wAu&-wA\\\hline -Au&A \end{array} \right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Given positive integer vectors $u,w$ with $Au\ge0$, $wA\ge0$, the $n\times n$ matrix $\widehat{A}$ bordering $A$ by $-Au$, $-wA$ and $wAu$.

nodes.name: Kernel generators of the extension
nodes.statement: The following vectors are primitive generators for the left and right kernels, respectively, of~$\widehat{A}$: \[ \phi=(1,w_1,w_2,\dots,w_{n-1}) \quad\text{and}\quad \delta=(1,u_1,u_2,\dots,u_{n-1}). \]
conclusions: The following vectors are primitive generators for the left and right kernels, respectively, of~$\widehat{A}$

nodes.name: Laplacian as extension of the reduced Laplacian
nodes.statement: Let~$L$ be the Laplacian matrix for a connected, undirected graph with respect to some ordering of the vertices, and let~$A=\tilde{L}$ be the corresponding reduced Laplacian with respect to the first vertex. Then~$A=A^t$ is an~$M$-matrix (\cite{Guzman}) with minimal burning script~$u=w=(1,\dots,1)$. The~$(w,u)$-extension of~$A$ recovers~$L$, i.e.,~$\widehat{A}=L$.

nodes.name: Divisor for an M-matrix
nodes.statement: A {\em divisor} is an element~$D\in\mathrm{Div}(\widehat{A}):=\mathbb{Z}^n$.

nodes.name: Degree for an M-matrix
nodes.statement: The {\em degree} of a divisor~$D$ is given by the dot product~$\deg(D):=\phi\cdot D$.

nodes.name: Linear equivalence for an M-matrix
nodes.statement: Define linear equivalence of divisors by~$D\sim D'$ if~$D-D'\in\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\widehat{A}$.

nodes.name: Picard and Jacobian groups of an M-matrix
nodes.statement: As before, let~$\mathrm{Pic}(\widehat{A}):=\mathbb{Z}^{n}/\!\sim$, which is graded by (our new) degree, and~$\mathrm{Jac}(\widehat{A}):=\mathrm{Pic}^{0}(\widehat{A})$, the group of divisor classes of divisors of degree~$0$.

nodes.name: Vertices as standard basis vectors
nodes.statement: For notational purposes, define~$v_i:=e_i$, the~$i$-th standard basis vector, for ~$i=1,\dots,n$.

nodes.name: Isomorphisms (1) and (2) for M-matrices
nodes.statement: The isomorphisms~\eqref{eqn: Pic(G)} and~\eqref{eqn: Jac(G)} of Section~\ref{sect: prelims} hold in this new setting in which~$\tilde{L}$ is replaced by~$A$.
conclusions: The isomorphisms~\eqref{eqn: Pic(G)} and~\eqref{eqn: Jac(G)} of Section~\ref{sect: prelims} hold in this new setting

nodes.name: Linear systems and lambda-generating function for an M-matrix
nodes.statement: For each divisor class~$[D]\in\mathrm{Pic}(\widehat{A})$, define the {\em complete linear system}~$|D|$, the set~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$, and the~$\lambda$-generating function~$\Lambda_{[D]}(z)$ as in Section~\ref{sect: prelims}.

nodes.name: Order of a vertex for an M-matrix
nodes.statement: Redefine~$\mathrm{ord}_q(v_i)$ to be the order of~$[v_i-\deg(v_i)q]\in\mathrm{Pic}(\widehat{A})$, and let~$\ell_i$ be any positive integer multiple of~$\mathrm{ord}_q(v_i)$.

nodes.name: Primary-secondary results for M-matrices
nodes.statement: Then Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}, Corollary~\ref{cor: ps-genfun}, and Proposition~\ref{prop: ps-computation} hold after replacing each occurrence of~$\ell_{v}$ with~$\phi_i\ell_i$.
conclusions: Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}, Corollary~\ref{cor: ps-genfun}, and Proposition~\ref{prop: ps-computation} hold after replacing each occurrence of~$\ell_{v}$ with~$\phi_i\ell_i$

nodes.name: Generating function for M-matrices via secondary divisors
nodes.statement: For instance, in Corollary~\ref{cor: ps-genfun}, we now have \begin{equation} \Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\frac{S(z)}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-z^{\phi_i\ell_i})} \end{equation} where~$S(z):=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}}z^{\deg(F)}$.
conclusions: \Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\frac{S(z)}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-z^{\phi_i\ell_i})}

nodes.name: Generating function with weighted denominators
nodes.statement: \Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\frac{S(z)}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-z^{\phi_i\ell_i})}
nodes.label: eqn: ps-genfun

nodes.name: Theorem 4.4 for M-matrices
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm: poly} then holds as stated, defining~$\deg(\omega):=\phi\cdot\omega$ in part~\ref{poly3}.
conclusions: Theorem~\ref{thm: poly} then holds as stated

nodes.name: Proposition 4.5 for M-matrices
nodes.statement: Proposition~\ref{prop: facet} holds by again replacing~$\ell_i$ by~$\phi_i\ell_i$ and redefining~$\mathrm{ord}_q(v_i)$ as discussed above.
conclusions: Proposition~\ref{prop: facet} holds

nodes.name: Multigrading by phi
nodes.statement: To generalize the results in Section~\ref{sect: molien}, take~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]$ to have the multigrading determined by~$\deg(x_i):=\phi_i$ for~$i=1,\dots,n$.

nodes.name: Modified representation rho for M-matrices
nodes.statement: The representation of~$\rho$, described in~(\ref{rho}), becomes \begin{equation} \rho(\chi)=(1,\chi([v_2-\deg(v_2)q]),\chi([v_3-\deg(v_3)q]),\dots,\chi([v_n-\deg(v_n)q])). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Modified representation rho
nodes.statement: \rho(\chi)=(1,\chi([v_2-\deg(v_2)q]),\chi([v_3-\deg(v_3)q]),\dots,\chi([v_n-\deg(v_n)q])).
nodes.label: eqn: new rho

nodes.name: Theorem 5.1 for M-matrices
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm: invariants} then extends with no changes to its statement.
conclusions: Theorem~\ref{thm: invariants} then extends with no changes to its statement

nodes.name: Multigraded Molien formula for M-matrices
nodes.statement: For Corollary~\ref{cor: lambda-molien}, use a multigraded version of Molien's theorem, for abelian groups, to get \begin{equation} \Lambda_{[D]}(z)= \Phi_{\Gamma,\chi}(z^{\phi_1},\dots,z^{\phi_n}) :=\frac{1}{|\mathrm{Jac}(\widehat{A})|}\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Jac}(\widehat{A})^*}\frac{\overline{\chi([D])}}{\det(I_n-\mathrm{diag}(z^{\phi_1},\dots,z^{\phi_n})\rho(\chi))} \end{equation} where~$\mathrm{diag}(\,\cdot\,)$ denotes the diagonal matrix with the given diagonal entries.
conclusions: \Lambda_{[D]}(z)= \Phi_{\Gamma,\chi}(z^{\phi_1},\dots,z^{\phi_n}) :=\frac{1}{|\mathrm{Jac}(\widehat{A})|}\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Jac}(\widehat{A})^*}\frac{\overline{\chi([D])}}{\det(I_n-\mathrm{diag}(z^{\phi_1},\dots,z^{\phi_n})\rho(\chi))}

nodes.name: Multigraded Molien series for M-matrices
nodes.statement: \Lambda_{[D]}(z)= \Phi_{\Gamma,\chi}(z^{\phi_1},\dots,z^{\phi_n}) :=\frac{1}{|\mathrm{Jac}(\widehat{A})|}\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Jac}(\widehat{A})^*}\frac{\overline{\chi([D])}}{\det(I_n-\mathrm{diag}(z^{\phi_1},\dots,z^{\phi_n})\rho(\chi))}
nodes.label: eqn: new lambda_molien

nodes.name: Root system Phi
nodes.statement: Let~$\Phi$ be a finite, crystallographic, irreducible root system.

nodes.name: Cartan matrices are M-matrices
nodes.statement: The Cartan matrix~$C$ for~$\Phi$ is an~$M$-matrix.
conclusions: The Cartan matrix~$C$ for~$\Phi$ is an~$M$-matrix.

nodes.name: Burning configurations of Cartan matrices
nodes.statement: Its burning configurations are the elements of the root lattice lying in the fundamental chamber (with respect to a choice of simple roots).
conclusions: Its burning configurations are the elements of the root lattice lying in the fundamental chamber

nodes.name: Extended Cartan matrix
nodes.statement: Making particular natural choices for burning configurations for~$C$ and its transpose~$C^t$, the authors define the extended Cartan matrix~$\widetilde{C}$, which is the Cartan matrix for the corresponding affine root system.

nodes.name: Picard group of the extended Cartan matrix is the fundamental group
nodes.statement: Letting~$A=C^t$ and~$\widehat{A}=\widetilde{C}^t$, it turns out that~$\mathrm{Pic}(\widehat{A})$ is the fundamental group of~$\Phi$, i.e., the quotient of the weight lattice by the root lattice.
conclusions: $\mathrm{Pic}(\widehat{A})$ is the fundamental group of~$\Phi$

nodes.name: Root system B_3
nodes.statement_short: For $B_3$: extension of the transposed Cartan matrix, $\mathrm{Jac}\simeq\mathbb{Z}/2$, primary/secondary divisors and both generating-function formulas.

nodes.name: Faithful representation rho
nodes.statement: Let~$\rho\colon\Gamma\to\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}^n)$ be a faithful representation of a finite group~$\Gamma$ with character~$\chi_{\rho}$.

nodes.name: Irreducible representations and characters
nodes.statement: Let~$\rho_1,\dots,\rho_n$ be the irreducible complex representations of~$\Gamma$, with~$\rho_1$ the trivial representation, and with respective characters~$\chi_1,\dots,\chi_n$.

nodes.name: Tensor product multiplicities m_ij
nodes.statement: For each~$i$, denote the character of the tensor product ~$\rho\otimes\rho_i$ by~$\chi_{\rho}\cdot\chi_i$, and define integers~$m_{ij}$ by \[ \chi_{\rho}\cdot\chi_i=\sum_{j=1}^nm_{ij}\chi_i. \]

nodes.name: Extended McKay-Cartan matrix
nodes.statement: Define the~$n\times n$ matrix~$M:=(m_{ij})$ and the {\em extended McKay-Cartan} matrix~$\widetilde{C}:=nI_n-M$.

nodes.name: McKay-Cartan matrix
nodes.statement: The {\em McKay-Cartan} matrix is then the submatrix~$C$ formed by removing the first row and first column of~$\widetilde{C}$.

nodes.name: Burning scripts for McKay-Cartan matrices
nodes.statement: The vectors $u=w=(\dim\rho_2,\dots,\dim\rho_n)$ are burning scripts for~$A$ and~$A^t$, with respect to which~$\widehat{A}=\widetilde{C}^t$ with left and right kernel generators \[ \phi = \delta = (\dim\rho_1,\dots,\dim\rho_n). \]
conclusions: $u=w=(\dim\rho_2,\dots,\dim\rho_n)$ are burning scripts for~$A$ and~$A^t$

nodes.name: McKay quiver
nodes.statement: The {\em McKay quiver} of~$\gamma$ is the directed graph with vertices~$\chi_1,\dots,\chi_n$ and~$m_{ij}$ directed edges from~$\chi_i$ to~$\chi_j$ for each~$i,j$.

nodes.name: McKay quiver of the representation rho for C_n
nodes.statement: Consider the representation~$\rho\colon\mathrm{Jac}(G)^*\to\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}^n)$ defined by~(\ref{rho}) of Section~\ref{sect: molien}. When~$G=C_n$, the cyclic graph on~$n$-vertices,~$\rho$ is the regular representation of the cyclic group $\mathrm{Jac}(G)^*\simeq\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Therefore,~$m_{ij}=1$ for all~$i,j$, the McKay quiver may be thought of as the (undirected) complete graph~$K_n$ on~$n$ vertices, and $\widehat{A}$ is its Laplacian matrix. Thus,~$\mathrm{Jac}(\widehat{A})=\mathrm{Jac}(K_n)$. More generally (\cite{BKR}, Section~6.2), the McKay quiver for any faithful complex representation~$\gamma$ of an abelian group has (directed) Laplacian matrix equal to the matrix~$\widehat{A}$ for~$\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: For $C_n$, $\rho$ is the regular representation of $\mathbb{Z}/n$, its McKay quiver is $K_n$ and $\mathrm{Jac}(\widehat{A})=\mathrm{Jac}(K_n)$.

nodes.name: McKay quivers of abelian groups
nodes.statement: More generally (\cite{BKR}, Section~6.2), the McKay quiver for any faithful complex representation~$\gamma$ of an abelian group has (directed) Laplacian matrix equal to the matrix~$\widehat{A}$ for~$\gamma$.
conclusions: the McKay quiver for any faithful complex representation~$\gamma$ of an abelian group has (directed) Laplacian matrix equal to the matrix~$\widehat{A}$ for~$\gamma$

nodes.name: Combinatorial bijections for arbitrary n and k
nodes.statement: Motivated by this work, \cite{Oh} finds a combinatorial bijection in the case~$D=kq$ when~$n$ is prime. It would be interesting to find combinatorial bijections for arbitrary~$n$ and~$k$.
nodes.statement_short: Find combinatorial bijections between $|D|$ on $C_n$ and binary necklaces for all $n,k$, not only $\gcd(n,k)=1$ or prime $n$.

nodes.name: Implications for root systems and representations
nodes.statement: It may be worthwhile to investigate the implications for each type of root system or for certain classes of representations.

nodes.name: Combinatorics of linear systems inside tropical cell complexes
nodes.statement: While we have determined this cardinality, one could hope to further describe the combinatorics of the complete linear system for a divisor on~$G$ within the cell complex for the associated divisor on~$\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Fix multiples $\ell_v$ of the orders and define $\mathcal{P}
nodes.statement: To prove part~\ref{ps-1}, for each~$v\in V$, let~$\ell_v$ be a positive multiple of~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$, and define~$\mathcal{P}$ and each~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ as in part~\ref{ps-2} of the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Fix multiples $\ell_v$ of the orders and define $\mathcal{P}$, $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ as in part (2)

nodes.name: Construct the decomposition by dividing each coefficient by
nodes.statement: Given~$E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$, for each~$v\in V$, let~$k_v$ be the largest integer such that~$E(v)-k_v\ell_v\geq0$, and define~$F:=E-\sum_{v\in V}k_v\ell_vv\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$. Then $E=F+\sum_{v\in V}k_v\ell_vv$ is a decomposition as required in part~\ref{ps-1}.
nodes.statement_short: Construct the decomposition by dividing each coefficient by $\ell_v$

nodes.name: Uniqueness: remainders in $[0,\ell_v)$ force equal quotients
nodes.statement: For uniqueness of this decomposition, suppose $E = F' + \sum_{v\in V}k_v'v$ for some~$F'\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ and~$k'_v\in\mathbb{N}$. Then for each~$v\in V$, we have~$0\leq F(v)=E(v)- k_v\ell_v<\ell_v$ and~$0\leq F'(v)=E(v)-k'_v\ell_v<\ell_v$. Subtracting these inequalities yields $-\ell_v<(k'_v-k_v)\ell_v<\ell_v$. It follows that~$k_v=k'_v$ for all~$v$ and~$F=F'$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness: remainders in $[0,\ell_v)$ force equal quotients

nodes.name: Recap sufficiency
nodes.statement: We have shown that if~$\mathcal{P}$ and~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ have the form displayed in~$\ref{ps-2}$, then they serve as sets of primary and secondary divisors, i.e., they satisfy the conditions in part~\ref{ps-1}. To show that necessity of this form and thus finish the proof of part~\ref{ps-2}, let~$\mathcal{P}$ and~$\{\mathcal{S}_{[D]}\}_{[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)}$ be any sets of primary and~$[D]$-secondary divisors.
nodes.statement_short: Recap sufficiency; set up necessity for arbitrary primary/secondary systems

nodes.name: Introduce the least $m_v$ with $m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v\notin\ma
nodes.statement: Since~$\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ is finite, for each~$v\in V$, there is a smallest natural number~$m_v$ such that~$m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v\notin\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the least $m_v$ with $m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v\notin\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$

nodes.name: Decompose $m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v$ as $av+bv$ with $b>0$
nodes.statement: Consider the primary-secondary decomposition~$m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v=F+\sum_{P\in\mathcal{P}}a_PP$. Since the divisors on the right-hand side are effective and all~$a_P$ are nonnegative, considering coefficients on both sides, it follows that decomposition takes the form~$m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v=av+bv$ for some~$a,b\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $av\in\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ and $bv\in\mathcal{P}$. By definition of~$m_v$, we must have~$b>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v$ as $av+bv$ with $b>0$

nodes.name: Both $a$ and $b$ are multiples of $\mathrm{ord}(v)$
nodes.statement: Since~$\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ and~$\mathcal{P}$ are subsets of~$\mathbb{E}_{[0]}$, we have~$av\sim aq$ and~$bv\sim bq$. Therefore,~$a=a'\mathrm{ord}(v)$ and~$b=b'\mathrm{ord}(v)$ for some~$a',b'\in\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Both $a$ and $b$ are multiples of $\mathrm{ord}(v)$

nodes.name: $a'\neq0$ contradicts disjointness of $\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ an
nodes.statement: If~$a'\neq0$, then~$b'<m_v$, which implies~$b'\mathrm{ord}(v)v\in\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ by definition of~$m_v$. However, that is impossible since the uniqueness of decompositions described in part~\ref{ps-1} implies~$\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ and~$\mathcal{P}$ are disjoint.
nodes.statement_short: $a'\neq0$ contradicts disjointness of $\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ and $\mathcal{P}$

nodes.name: Conclude $\mathcal{P}=\{\ell_v v\}$ by linear independence,
nodes.statement: Defining~$\ell_v:=m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)$, it follows that~$\ell_v v\in\mathcal{P}$ for all~$v$. However, again by uniqueness of decompositions, the elements of~$\mathcal{P}$ must be linearly independent over~$\mathbb{Z}$, which implies there are no other primary divisors. So~$\mathcal{P}=\left\{ \ell_v:v\in V \right\}$, as claimed, and it is then straightforward to show that~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ must have the form stated in~\ref{ps-2} for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $\mathcal{P}=\{\ell_v v\}$ by linear independence, and the form of $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$

nodes.name: Encode $\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ as a multivariate generating serie
nodes.statement: Introduce indeterminates~$\left\{ x_v \right\}_{v\in V}$, and identify each effective divisor~$E$ with a monomial~$x^E:=\prod_{v\in V}x_v^{E(v)}$. Define \[ \sigma_D(x)=\sum_{E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}}x^{E}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Encode $\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ as a multivariate generating series $\sigma_D$

nodes.name: Factor each monomial via the primary-secondary decomposition
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}, we may uniquely write \[ x^E=x^F\cdot\prod_{P\in\mathcal{P}}x^{a_PP} =x^F\cdot\prod_{v\in V}x_v^{a_v\ell_v} \] for some~$F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ and~$a_v\geq0$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor each monomial via the primary-secondary decomposition

nodes.name: Sum geometric series in each variable
nodes.statement: Then \begin{align*} \sigma_D(x)&=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}}x^F\sum_{a\in \mathbb{N}^V}\prod_{v\in V}x_v^{a_v\ell_v} =\left(\sum_{F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}}x^F\right)\prod_{v\in V}\left(1+x_v^{\ell_v}+x_v^{2\ell_v} +\dots\right)\\[8pt] &=\left(\sum_{F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}}x^F\right)\prod_{v\in V}\frac{1}{1-x_v^{\ell_v}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Sum geometric series in each variable

nodes.name: Specialize all variables to $z$
nodes.statement: Now note that $\Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\sigma_D(z,z,\dots,z)$ to conclude the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize all variables to $z$

nodes.name: Part (1): $\mathrm{ord}_q(v)$ is the least $k$ with $\tilde{
nodes.statement: First note that~$\tilde{L}$ has rank~$n-1$, and thus has an inverse~$\tilde{L}^{-1}$ over~$\mathbb{Q}$. By~\eqref{eqn: Jac(G)} of Section~\ref{sect: prelims}, the order of~$[v-q]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ is the least positive integer~$k$ such that~$kv\in\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}$. Therefore,~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ is the least positive integer~$k$ such that~$\tilde{L}^{-1}(kv)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$. Part~\ref{ps-comp1} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Part (1): $\mathrm{ord}_q(v)$ is the least $k$ with $\tilde{L}^{-1}(kv)$ integral

nodes.name: Part (2): standard representatives of $H_{[D]}$ are exactly
nodes.statement: Part~\ref{ps-comp2} is immediate: a divisor~$E$ is a standard representative for an element in~$H_{[D]}$ if and only if $E|_{q=0}=D|_{q=0} \bmod\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}$ and $0\leq E(v)<\ell_v$ for all~$v\in V$, which is exactly the requirement for being an element of~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (2): standard representatives of $H_{[D]}$ are exactly the secondary divisors

nodes.name: Part (3): count secondary divisors via a surjection onto $\m
nodes.statement: Now consider part~\ref{ps-comp3}. Since~$\ell_v[v-q]=[0]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ for all~$v$, there is a surjection \[ \textstyle {\mathbb{Z}}^n/\prod_{v\in V}\ell_v\mathbb{Z}\to\mathrm{Jac}(G)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}/\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L} \] which sends the class of the~$v$-th standard basis vector to~$[v-q]$. Its kernel is~$H_{[0]}$. So by part~\ref{ps-comp2}, we have $|\mathcal{S}_{[0]}||\mathrm{Jac}(G)|=\prod_{v\in V}\ell_v$. However, for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, there is a well-defined bijection \begin{align*} H_{[0]}&\to H_{[D]}\\ \pi(E)&\mapsto\pi(D+E). \end{align*} So~$|\mathcal{S}_{[D]}|=|\mathcal{S}_{[0]}|$, and part~\ref{ps-comp3} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Part (3): count secondary divisors via a surjection onto $\mathrm{Jac}(G)$

nodes.name: Surjection from $\mathbb{Z}^n/\prod\ell_v\mathbb{Z}$ onto $\
nodes.statement: Now consider part~\ref{ps-comp3}. Since~$\ell_v[v-q]=[0]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ for all~$v$, there is a surjection \[ \textstyle {\mathbb{Z}}^n/\prod_{v\in V}\ell_v\mathbb{Z}\to\mathrm{Jac}(G)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}/\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L} \] which sends the class of the~$v$-th standard basis vector to~$[v-q]$.
nodes.statement_short: Surjection from $\mathbb{Z}^n/\prod\ell_v\mathbb{Z}$ onto $\mathrm{Jac}(G)$

nodes.name: Kernel is $H_{[0]}$, so $|\mathcal{S}_{[0]}||\mathrm{Jac}(G)
nodes.statement: Its kernel is~$H_{[0]}$. So by part~\ref{ps-comp2}, we have $|\mathcal{S}_{[0]}||\mathrm{Jac}(G)|=\prod_{v\in V}\ell_v$.
nodes.statement_short: Kernel is $H_{[0]}$, so $|\mathcal{S}_{[0]}||\mathrm{Jac}(G)|=\prod\ell_v$ by part (2)

nodes.name: Translation bijection $H_{[0]}\to H_{[D]}$ gives the count f
nodes.statement: However, for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, there is a well-defined bijection \begin{align*} H_{[0]}&\to H_{[D]}\\ \pi(E)&\mapsto\pi(D+E). \end{align*} So~$|\mathcal{S}_{[D]}|=|\mathcal{S}_{[0]}|$, and part~\ref{ps-comp3} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Translation bijection $H_{[0]}\to H_{[D]}$ gives the count for every class

nodes.name: Compute each $\mathrm{ord}_q(v)$ from the columns of $\tilde
nodes.statement: To summarize the above: in order to compute a set of primary divisors, use Proposition~\ref{prop: ps-computation} to compute each~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ for~$v\neq q$ from the columns of~$\tilde{L}^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute each $\mathrm{ord}_q(v)$ from the columns of $\tilde{L}^{-1}$

nodes.name: Choose $\ell_v$ as multiples of the orders
nodes.statement: Then take~$\mathcal{P}=\{ \ell_v v \}_{v\in V}$ where the~$\ell_v$ are arbitrary positive multiples of the corresponding~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\ell_v$ as multiples of the orders; primary divisors $\ell_v v$

nodes.name: Optionally take $\ell_v=\mathrm{ord}_q(v)$ to minimize secon
nodes.statement: In order to minimize the number of secondary divisors, one would take~$\ell_v=\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ for each~$v$. In particular, this would mean~$\ell_q=\mathrm{ord}_{q}(q)=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Optionally take $\ell_v=\mathrm{ord}_q(v)$ to minimize secondary divisors

nodes.name: Use Proposition 3.4(2) to compute $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$
nodes.statement: Next, use part~\ref{ps-comp2} of Proposition~\ref{prop: ps-computation} to compute~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Use Proposition 3.4(2) to compute $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$

nodes.name: Compute the column Hermite normal form $A$ of $\tilde{L}$
nodes.statement: To ease the computation of~$\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}$, perform invertible integer column operations on~$\tilde{L}$ to compute its Hermite normal form~$A$. (We will always take ``Hermite normal form'' to mean ``column Hermite normal form''.)
nodes.statement_short: Compute the column Hermite normal form $A$ of $\tilde{L}$

nodes.name: Find standard representatives of the coset $D|_{q=0}+\mathrm
nodes.statement: Then find the set~$S$ of standard representatives for the coset $D|_{q=0}+\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}A$ modulo $\prod_{v\in V\setminus\left\{ q \right\}}\ell_v\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: Find standard representatives of the coset $D|_{q=0}+\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}A$

nodes.name: Append $kq$, $0\le k<\ell_q$, to obtain $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$
nodes.statement: Finally~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}=\left\{ c+kq:c\in S \text{ and } 0\leq k <\ell_q\right\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Append $kq$, $0\le k<\ell_q$, to obtain $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$

nodes.name: Rewrite $\mathcal{K}_D$ using $\tilde{L}$ and the truncated
nodes.statement: Let~$\tilde{r}_n\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ denote the last row of~$L$ with its last entry removed. Then \begin{equation} \mathcal{K}_D = \left\{ (f,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{R}: \tilde{L} f\geq -D|_{q=0}\text{ and }\tilde{r}_n\cdot f+t\geq-D(q)\right\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $\mathcal{K}_D$ using $\tilde{L}$ and the truncated last row $\tilde{r}_n$

nodes.name: Independent defining inequalities give a rational simplicial
nodes.statement: Since~$\tilde{L}$ is invertible, these defining conditions are independent, and it follows that~$\mathcal{K}_D$ is a rational~$n$-cone.
nodes.statement_short: Independent defining inequalities give a rational simplicial cone

nodes.name: Solve for the apex
nodes.statement: To find the apex, first solve~$\tilde{L} f=-D|_{q=0}$ to find~$f=\tilde{L}^{-1}(-D|_{q=0})$. Next, since the sum of the rows of~$L$ is~$0$, if follows that~$\tilde{r}_n\cdot f=-\tilde{L} f$, and it is now easy to verify that the last coordinate of the apex is~$t=0$ using the fact that~$\deg(D)=0$. The rest follows immediately from the discussion preceding the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Solve for the apex; its last coordinate is $0$ since $\deg(D)=0$

nodes.name: Part (1): unique firing-script representative with last coor
nodes.statement: Part~\ref{poly1} uses the fact that every firing script has a unique representative modulo $\ker L$ having final coordinate~$0$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (1): unique firing-script representative with last coordinate $0$

nodes.name: Part (2): apply the unique lattice-point decomposition
nodes.statement: Part~\ref{poly2} relies on Property~\ref{property: characterization}.
nodes.statement_short: Part (2): apply the unique lattice-point decomposition

nodes.name: Part (3): degree of $\psi_D(f,k)$ is $k$
nodes.statement: Part~\ref{poly3} follows since~$\deg\psi_D(f,k)=k$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (3): degree of $\psi_D(f,k)$ is $k$

nodes.name: Membership reduces to $\tilde{L}f\ge -D|_{q=0}$
nodes.statement: We have~$f\in\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D$ if and only if \[ \tilde{L} f\geq-D|_{q=0}\quad\text{and}\quad \tilde{r}_n\cdot f\geq -D(q)-k \] for some~$k\in\mathbb{N}$. The second condition is superfluous since~$k$ can be arbitrarily large.
nodes.statement_short: Membership reduces to $\tilde{L}f\ge -D|_{q=0}$; the last inequality is superfluous

nodes.name: Invertibility of $\tilde{L}$ gives the simplicial cone and i
nodes.statement: The fact that~$\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}$ is a rational simplicial~$(n-1)$-cone with apex~$\tilde{L}^{-1}(-D|_{q=0})$ follows since~$\tilde{L}$ is invertible. This establishes part~\ref{facet1}.
nodes.statement_short: Invertibility of $\tilde{L}$ gives the simplicial cone and its apex: part (1)

nodes.name: Part (2) from part (1) and the description (4) of $\mathcal{
nodes.statement: Part~\ref{facet2} then follows from part~\ref{facet1} and the description of~$\mathcal{K}_D$ given in~\eqref{eqn: K_D} in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm: poly}.
nodes.statement_short: Part (2) from part (1) and the description (4) of $\mathcal{K}_D$

nodes.name: Part (3) from Theorem 4.4(2) and Theorem 3.1(2)
nodes.statement: Since~$K_D=\imath_D{\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}q$, part~\ref{facet3} follows from Theorem~\ref{thm: poly}~\ref{poly2} and Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}~\ref{ps-2}.
nodes.statement_short: Part (3) from Theorem 4.4(2) and Theorem 3.1(2)

nodes.name: Expand an arbitrary polynomial in the monomials $x^E$
nodes.statement: An arbitrary element of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]$ may be written as~$f=\sum^{\,}_{E}a_Ex^E$ where the sum is over all effective divisors of~$G$ and all but finitely many~$a_E$ are zero.
nodes.statement_short: Expand an arbitrary polynomial in the monomials $x^E$

nodes.name: Compute $f\circ\rho(\chi)$: each $x^E$ is scaled by $\chi([E
nodes.statement: Let~$\chi\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)^{*}$. Then \allowdisplaybreaks \begin{align*} f\circ\rho(\chi) &= \sum_{E}a^{\,}_E(x^E\circ\rho(\chi))\\ &= \sum_{E}a^{\,}_E\textstyle\left(\prod_{v\in V}\chi([v-q])^{E(v)} \right)x^E\\ &= \sum_{E}a^{\,}_E\textstyle\,\chi\!\left(\sum_{v\in V}E(v)([v-q])\right)x^E\\ &= \sum_{E}a^{\,}_E\textstyle\,\chi\!\left([E-\deg(E)q]\right)x^E. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Compute $f\circ\rho(\chi)$: each $x^E$ is scaled by $\chi([E-\deg(E)q])$

nodes.name: $[D]$-invariance holds iff all monomials come from $\mathbb{
nodes.statement: Therefore,~$f\in\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{[D]}$ if and only if for each~$E$ such that~$a^{\,}_E\neq0$, we have $\chi([E-\deg(E)q])=\chi([D])$ for all~$\chi$, or equivalently, $[E-\deg(E)q]=[D]$, i.e.,~$E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$.
nodes.statement_short: $[D]$-invariance holds iff all monomials come from $\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$

nodes.name: All three parts follow
nodes.statement: Parts~\ref{inv1},~\ref{inv2}, and~\ref{inv3} follow. Part~\ref{inv2} reflects the fact that the~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ partition the set of effective divisors.
nodes.statement_short: All three parts follow; part (2) reflects the partition of effective divisors

nodes.name: Reduce $\tilde{L}$ to diagonal (Smith) form $M$
nodes.statement: To compute with Corollary~\ref{cor: lambda-molien} concretely, use integer row and column operations to reduce~$\tilde{L}$ to diagonal form (e.g., Smith normal form), denoting the result by~$M:=\mathrm{diag}(m_1,\dots,m_{n-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce $\tilde{L}$ to diagonal (Smith) form $M$

nodes.name: Record the operations in $U$, $W$ with $U\tilde{L}W=M$
nodes.statement: Record the row and column operations in matrices~$U$ and~$W$ so that~$U\tilde{L} W = M$.
nodes.statement_short: Record the operations in $U$, $W$ with $U\tilde{L}W=M$

nodes.name: Identify $\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ with $\prod\mathbb{Z}/m_i\mathbb{
nodes.statement: Then~$U$ descends to an isomorphism \[ \mathrm{Jac}(G)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}/\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}\xrightarrow{\ U\ }\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\mathbb{Z}/m_i\mathbb{Z}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ with $\prod\mathbb{Z}/m_i\mathbb{Z}$ via $U$

nodes.name: Lift each $r\in R$ and form $\tilde{r}$
nodes.statement: Having identified~$\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ with~$R:=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\mathbb{Z}/m_i\mathbb{Z}$, we now describe the characters. For each~$r\in R$, choose a representative lifting~$(r_1,\dots,r_{n-1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$, and let $ \tilde{r} := \left(\frac{r_1}{m_1},\dots,\frac{r_{n-1}}{m_{n-1}} \right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift each $r\in R$ and form $\tilde{r}$

nodes.name: Define the character $\tilde{\chi}_r$
nodes.statement: Define the character~$\tilde{\chi}_r\in R^*$ by \[ \tilde{\chi}_r(a) :=\exp(2\pi i\,(\tilde{r}\cdot a)) \] for each~$a\in R$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the character $\tilde{\chi}_r$

nodes.name: Pull back to the character $\chi_r$ of $\mathrm{Jac}(G)$
nodes.statement: Then define~$\chi_r\in\mathrm{Jac}^*(G)$ by \[ \chi_r([D]):=\tilde{\chi}_r(U(D|_{q=0})) \] for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pull back to the character $\chi_r$ of $\mathrm{Jac}(G)$

nodes.name: Express $\rho(\chi_r)$ via the columns of $U$
nodes.statement: It follows that \[ \rho(\chi_r)=\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{\chi}_r(u_1),\tilde{\chi}_r(u_2),\dots,\tilde{\chi}_r(u_{n-1}),1) \] where~$u_j$ is the~$j$-th column of~$U$.
nodes.statement_short: Express $\rho(\chi_r)$ via the columns of $U$

nodes.name: Drop trivial factors with $m_k=1$
nodes.statement: In all of the above, if~$m_k=1$ for some~$k$, then the~$k$-th factor of~$R$ and the~$k$-th {\em row} of~$U$ may be dropped.
nodes.statement_short: Drop trivial factors with $m_k=1$

nodes.name: Fix $N$ and a word for its code
nodes.statement: Let~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$, and let~$a=a_N=a_1\dots a_n$ be a representative word for $\mathrm{code}(N)$. We first show that~$N$ is~$m_j$-divisible if and only if~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n_j$-divisible.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $N$ and a word for its code; aim at part (1)

nodes.name: Relate periods: $n=p\ell$, period of $N$ is $\ell+\alpha$, $
nodes.statement: Let~$\ell$ be the period of~$\mathrm{code}(N)$. Then since the length of the necklace~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n$, there is an integer~$p$ such that~$n=p\ell$. The period of~$N$ is~$\ell+\alpha$ where~$\alpha:=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}a_i$. Since~$\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i=k$, and the period of~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$\ell$, it follows that~$p\alpha=k$.
nodes.statement_short: Relate periods: $n=p\ell$, period of $N$ is $\ell+\alpha$, $p\alpha=k$

nodes.name: $m_j$-divisibility of $N$ is equivalent to $p\mid j$
nodes.statement: Therefore, \begin{align*} \text{$N$ is~$m_j$-divisible}&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \left( \frac{n+k}{\gcd(n,k,j)}\right)\bigg|\,(\ell+\alpha)\\[8pt] &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{p(\ell+\alpha)}{\gcd(p\ell,p\alpha,j)}\bigg|\,(\ell+\alpha)\\[8pt] &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{\gcd(p\ell,p\alpha,j)}{p(\ell+\alpha)}\cdot(\ell+\alpha)\in\mathbb{Z}\\[8pt] &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p|j. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $m_j$-divisibility of $N$ is equivalent to $p\mid j$

nodes.name: $n_j$-divisibility of the code is also equivalent to $p\mid
nodes.statement: Similarly, \[ \text{$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n_j$-divisible} \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad\left( \frac{n}{\gcd(n,j)} \right)\bigg|\,\ell \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\frac{p\ell}{\gcd(p\ell,j)}\bigg|\,\ell \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad p|j. \]
nodes.statement_short: $n_j$-divisibility of the code is also equivalent to $p\mid j$

nodes.name: Part (2): $f_N$ is $[D_j]$-invariant by construction
nodes.statement: Continuing with the notation already established, we now prove part~\ref{basis part2}. Since~$f_N$ is defined using the Reynolds operator, it is~$[D_j]$-invariant.
nodes.statement_short: Part (2): $f_N$ is $[D_j]$-invariant by construction

nodes.name: Claim: $y^a$ appears in $f_N$ with nonzero coefficient
nodes.statement: To see that it is non-zero, we show that the monomial~$y^a$ appears in~$f_N$ with a nonzero coefficient. We have~$y^a=y^{\sigma^i(a)}$ if and only if~$i$ is a multiple of the period~$\ell$. However,~$\ell$ is divisible by~$n_j$, which is the order of~$\omega^{j}$. So the coefficient of~$y^{\sigma^i(a)}$ in the expression for the Reynolds operator is~$\omega^{-ij}/n=1/n$. Therefore, the coefficient of~$y^{a}$ in~$f_N$ is the integer~$p/n=1/\ell\neq0$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: $y^a$ appears in $f_N$ with nonzero coefficient

nodes.name: Shifts fixing $y^a$ are multiples of $\ell$, divisible by th
nodes.statement: We have~$y^a=y^{\sigma^i(a)}$ if and only if~$i$ is a multiple of the period~$\ell$. However,~$\ell$ is divisible by~$n_j$, which is the order of~$\omega^{j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Shifts fixing $y^a$ are multiples of $\ell$, divisible by the order of $\omega^j$

nodes.name: The coefficient of $y^a$ is $1/\ell\neq0$
nodes.statement: So the coefficient of~$y^{\sigma^i(a)}$ in the expression for the Reynolds operator is~$\omega^{-ij}/n=1/n$. Therefore, the coefficient of~$y^{a}$ in~$f_N$ is the integer~$p/n=1/\ell\neq0$.
nodes.statement_short: The coefficient of $y^a$ is $1/\ell\neq0$

nodes.name: Hence $f_N$ is a nonzero invariant of degree $k$
nodes.statement: It now follows that~$f_N$ has degree~$k$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $f_N$ is a nonzero invariant of degree $k$

nodes.name: The $f_N$ have disjoint monomial supports, hence are indepen
nodes.statement: Let~$\mathcal{B}$ be the set of~$f_N$ as~$N$ varies over~$m_j$-divisible elements of~$\mathcal{N}(n,k)$. Distinct elements of~$\mathcal{B}$ share no monomials in common, and hence~$\mathcal{B}$ is a linearly independent set.
nodes.statement_short: The $f_N$ have disjoint monomial supports, hence are independent

nodes.name: Assume a homogeneous invariant $h$ outside the span
nodes.statement: To show~$\mathcal{B}$ spans the relative invariant module and finish the proof, let~$h\in\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$ be a homogeneous~$[D_j]$-invariant of degree~$k$. For the sake of contradiction, suppose~$h\notin\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a homogeneous invariant $h$ outside the span

nodes.name: Take such $h$ with fewest terms and a term $\beta y^b$
nodes.statement: We regard~$h$ as a sum of terms where each term is a nonzero constant times a monomial, and the monomials are distinct. Among all elements of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$ that are not in~$\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})$, let~$h$ be one with the fewest number of terms, and let~~$\beta y^b$ be one of these terms. Then~$\beta\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b)$ is a sum of terms appearing in~$h$.
nodes.statement_short: Take such $h$ with fewest terms and a term $\beta y^b$

nodes.name: Compute the coefficient of $y^b$ in $\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b
nodes.statement: Let~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ be the necklace with~$\mathrm{code}(N)=[b]$. Say~$[b]$ has period~$m$ and write~$n=mq$ for some integer~$q$. The coefficient of~$y^b$ in~$\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b)$ is \[ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^q(\omega^{-jm})^i, \] and the order of~$\omega^{-jm}$ is~$q/\gcd(q,j)$, a divisor of~$q$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the coefficient of $y^b$ in $\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b)$ as a root-of-unity sum

nodes.name: Non-divisibility would make that sum vanish, so $[b]$ is $n_
nodes.statement: If~$[b]$ is not~$n_j$-divisible, then the order of~$\omega^j$ does not divide~$m$, and hence,~$\omega^{jm}\neq1$. It would then follow that the above sum is~$0$, which contradicts the fact that~$\beta y^b$ is a term of~$h$. Therefore,~$[b]$ is~$n_j$-divisible and~$\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b)=f_N\in\mathcal{B}$.
nodes.statement_short: Non-divisibility would make that sum vanish, so $[b]$ is $n_j$-divisible and $\mathcal{R}(y^b)=f_N$

nodes.name: $h-\beta f_N$ has fewer terms: contradiction, so $\mathcal{B
nodes.statement: However, then the polynomial~$h-\beta f_N$ is an element of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$ with fewer terms than~$h$ and not in~$\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})$, which is a contradiction. So~$\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})=\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$.
nodes.statement_short: $h-\beta f_N$ has fewer terms: contradiction, so $\mathcal{B}$ spans

nodes.name: Laplacian columns are orthogonal to $\eta$ modulo $n$
nodes.statement: First note that if~$c$ is a column of the Laplacian matrix for~$C_n$, then~$c\cdot\eta=0\bmod n$.
nodes.statement_short: Laplacian columns are orthogonal to $\eta$ modulo $n$

nodes.name: Write $D\sim D_i+mq$
nodes.statement: Given any~$D\in\mathrm{Div}(C_n)$, there exists~$i$ and~$m$ such that~$D\sim D_i+mq$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $D\sim D_i+mq$

nodes.name: Compute $D\cdot\vec1=m$ and $D\cdot\eta\equiv i$
nodes.statement: Then~$D\cdot\vec{1}=m$, and \[ D\cdot\eta = (D_i+mq)\cdot\eta\bmod n= i\bmod n. \] The result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $D\cdot\vec1=m$ and $D\cdot\eta\equiv i$

nodes.name: Injectivity: equal necklaces come from rotated divisors $E'=
nodes.statement: Let~$\eta=(1,2,\dots,n)$ as in Lemma~\ref{lemma: divisors on C_n}. To show injectivity, suppose~$\psi(E)=\psi(E')$ for some pair of effective divisors~$E,E'\in\mathrm{Div}^k(C_n)$. It follows that~$E'=\sigma^i(E)$ for some~$i$.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity: equal necklaces come from rotated divisors $E'=\sigma^i(E)$

nodes.name: Lemma 6.6 gives $j=j+ik$ mod $n$, so $i\equiv0$ when $\gcd(n
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lemma: divisors on C_n}, working modulo~$n$, \[ j = E'\cdot\eta =\sigma^i(E)\cdot\eta=E\cdot(\eta+i\vec{1})=j+ik\bmod n. \] If~$\gcd(n,k)=1$, it follows that~$i=0\bmod n$, and hence~$E=E'$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.6 gives $j=j+ik$ mod $n$, so $i\equiv0$ when $\gcd(n,k)=1$

nodes.name: Surjectivity: take the divisor $E$ read off from the code
nodes.statement: For surjectivity, let~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ with~$\mathrm{code}(N)=[a_1\dots a_n]$. Let~$E:=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathrm{Div}^k(C_n)$, and say~$E\cdot\eta=m\bmod n$.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity: take the divisor $E$ read off from the code

nodes.name: Rotate $E$ so that it lands in $|D_j+kq|$
nodes.statement: Then $\sigma^i(E)\cdot\eta=m+ik\bmod n$ for each~$i$. If~$\gcd(n,k)=1$, we can take~$i$ so that~$m+ik=j\bmod n$ and define~$E':=\sigma^i(E)$. Then~$E'\in|D_j+kq|$ and~$\psi(E')=N$.
nodes.statement_short: Rotate $E$ so that it lands in $|D_j+kq|$

nodes.name: Start from the all-ones vector
nodes.statement: start with~$u=(1,\dots,1)$
nodes.statement_short: Start from the all-ones vector

nodes.name: While some $(Au)_i<0$, increment $u_i$
nodes.statement: then as long as~$(Au)_i<0$ for some~$i$, increase~$u_i$ by~$1$
nodes.statement_short: While some $(Au)_i<0$, increment $u_i$
